findings.summary: Google's doorway pages policy has been on the books since 2015 and remains in the current spam policies documentation verbatim. The March 2024 spam update introduced two new adjacent policies — scaled content abuse and site reputation abuse — that overlap directly with programmatic location-page strategies. Enforcement is primarily algorithmic via SpamBrain and core ranking systems (doorway pages) or a mix of manual action and algorithmic systems (scaled content and site reputation abuse). The helpful content classifier was folded into the core ranking system in March 2024, meaning unhelpfulness is now a persistent, continuously evaluated signal rather than a discrete named update. The October 2022 spam update specifically deindexed near-duplicate location pages at scale, giving local-SEO operators an early warning that location pages are an active enforcement target.
key_findings: DOORWAY PAGES — VERBATIM POLICY (current, developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies): 'Doorway abuse is when sites or pages are created to rank for specific, similar search queries. They lead users to intermediate pages that are not as useful as the final destination.' The policy lists four specific examples: (1) Having multiple websites with slight variations to the URL and home page to maximize their reach for any specific query; (2) Having multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page; (3) Generating pages to funnel visitors into the actual usable or relevant portion of a site; (4) Creating substantially similar pages that are closer to search results than a clearly defined, browseable hierarchy.

SCALED CONTENT ABUSE — VERBATIM DEFINITION (introduced March 2024, current in spam policies page): 'Scaled content abuse is when many pages are generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users. This abusive practice is typically focused on creating large amounts of unoriginal content that provides little to no value to users, no matter how it's created.' The phrase 'no matter how it's created' was a deliberate addition that explicitly extends the policy to AI-generated, automation-assisted, and human-written content alike. What changed from prior policy: this replaced the older 'spammy automatically generated content' entry and broadened it to cover AI-generated at scale. Source: developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies.

SITE REPUTATION ABUSE — VERBATIM DEFINITION (introduced March 2024, clarified November 2024): 'Site reputation abuse is when third-party pages are published with little or no first-party oversight or involvement, where the purpose is to manipulate Search rankings by taking advantage of the first-party site's ranking signals. Such third-party pages include sponsored, advertising, partner, or other third-party pages that are typically independent of a host site's main purpose or produced without close oversight or involvement of the host site, and provide little to no value to users.' What changed: this was a new policy in March 2024 targeting parasite SEO; enforcement was initially manual-action-only; November 2024 update clarified scope. Source: developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/11/site-reputation-abuse.

ENFORCEMENT MECHANICS — DOORWAY PAGES: Primarily algorithmic. SpamBrain (Google's AI-based spam prevention system, deployed since at least 2018 and continuously retrained) identifies funneling patterns at scale. Doorway page demotion typically manifests as automatic deindexing of affected pages or ranking suppression — not a manual action notification in Search Console. The October 2022 spam update is the clearest public case: service-area business sites with near-duplicate city location pages saw pages automatically deindexed, causing rank drops. No manual action warning was issued — pages simply dropped out of the index.

ENFORCEMENT MECHANICS — SCALED CONTENT ABUSE: Dual track. Google announced in March 2024 that it would 'take action against scaled content abuse both through algorithmic spam systems and manual actions.' Manual actions appear in Search Console; algorithmic demotions do not. The March 2024 spam update rolled out over roughly two weeks (March 5 – April 19, 2024).

ENFORCEMENT MECHANICS — HELPFUL CONTENT / CORE RANKING: As of March 2024, the formerly discrete helpful content update classifier was merged into the core ranking system. This means unhelpfulness is now a continuously evaluated, persistent signal — not a separate named update — and runs in parallel with all other ranking factors. Sites with large volumes of low-value templated pages accumulate a site-level unhelpfulness signal that suppresses rankings broadly, not just on the specific low-quality pages.

HELPFUL CONTENT SYSTEM HISTORY RELEVANT TO LOCATION PAGES: The helpful content classifier originally launched August 2022 evaluated entire sites, not just individual pages. A site with substantial unhelpful content could see its entire domain's rankings suppressed, including otherwise-useful pages. This site-wide suppression mechanism makes a large set of thin location pages especially dangerous — they pull down the whole domain.

GOOGLE'S OWN DIAGNOSTIC QUESTIONS FOR DOORWAY PAGES (from the March 2015 doorway pages update blog post, still authoritative): 'Is the purpose to optimize for search engines and funnel visitors into the actual usable or relevant portion of your site, or are they an integral part of your site's user experience? Do the pages duplicate useful aggregations of items (locations, products, etc.) that already exist on the site for the purpose of capturing more search traffic? Are the pages meant to rank for generic terms yet the content provided is extremely specific? Do the pages exist as an island? Are they difficult to navigate to from other parts of your site?' Source: developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages.

OCTOBER 2022 SPAM UPDATE — LOCATION PAGE PRECEDENT: Search Engine Land documented that service-area businesses saw rank volatility tied to the October 2022 spam update; the common thread was duplicate-content location pages (i.e., doorway pages). Google did not issue manual action notices; pages were automatically deindexed. This is the clearest historical proof that Google's spam system acts against city-swapped location pages algorithmically and silently. Source: searchengineland.com/location-pages-google-october-spam-update-390016.

## What Specifically Triggers the Doorway-Page Flag

The following are the concrete signals Google's systems (SpamBrain, core ranking, scaled-content-abuse classifiers) use to identify location pages as doorways. Sources listed after each item.

**Content signals**

- **Town-name-only swap test fails.** If removing the city name and replacing it with any other city produces a page that says exactly the same thing, the pages are doorways. Google's 2015 diagnostic question is verbatim: are the pages intended to rank for generic terms while the content is extremely specific only in the swapped token? ([developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages))

- **Near-duplicate body copy at scale.** Dozens or hundreds of pages with identical or near-identical body text, identical section structure, identical FAQ answers, identical brand/material lists, and identical process steps — distinguished only by a location token — directly match the four doorway examples in the current spam policy. ([developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies))

- **No locally unique content.** No information that is true of Apex and not of Cary. No data, imagery, testimonials, project references, permit notes, or competitive context that is specific to the town. Google's diagnostic asks: is the page "an integral part of the site's user experience" or does it exist purely to capture a search query? ([developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages))

- **Large amounts of unoriginal content regardless of generation method.** The scaled content abuse policy (March 2024) explicitly covers pages that are "unoriginal content that provides little to no value to users, no matter how it's created" — AI, templates, human copy-paste, all treated equally. ([developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies))

**Structural / site-architecture signals**

- **All pages funnel to one destination.** Every city page ultimately points to the same contact form, the same phone number, the same CTA, and offers no browseable path within the city page itself. This is the second example in Google's verbatim doorway definition: "multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page." ([developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies))

- **Island pages — not integrated into site hierarchy.** Pages that are not linked from any contextual content, not discoverable through a logical site browsing path, and exist solely as entry points from search. Google's diagnostic: "Are the pages meant to exist as an island?" ([developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages))

- **Rapid URL-count inflation without corresponding content depth.** Google's internal QualityCopiaFireflySiteSignal system (documented by Hobo Web) reportedly measures the ratio of URLs generated in a period against the substantive content produced. A site that publishes 30 city pages in a week where each has only a city swap carries a sharp URL-to-substance ratio spike. ([hobo-web.co.uk/firefly/](https://www.hobo-web.co.uk/firefly/))

**Behavioral / engagement signals**

- **High bounce / low dwell time on city pages.** SpamBrain incorporates engagement signals. If users land on a city page, quickly return to the SERP (pogosticking), and never visit deeper pages, that negative engagement corroborates the thin-content classifier signal. ([searchxpro.com/how-google-detects-content-spam-in-2025/](https://searchxpro.com/how-google-detects-content-spam-in-2025/))

**Site-level compounding signal**

- **Volume of low-value pages pulling down the whole domain.** The helpful content system (now merged into core ranking, March 2024) evaluates content quality at the site level. A large batch of doorway-pattern city pages depresses the site-wide helpfulness score, suppressing rankings for every page on the domain — not just the doorway pages themselves. ([developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies))

**Documented enforcement precedent specific to location pages**

- **October 2022 spam update** automatically deindexed near-duplicate city pages on service-area business sites with no manual action warning. Pages simply disappeared from the index. This is the clearest proof that the enforcement is silent, algorithmic, and triggered by the doorway-page pattern in location-page form. ([searchengineland.com/location-pages-google-october-spam-update-390016](https://searchengineland.com/location-pages-google-october-spam-update-390016))

findings.summary: Google draws the legitimacy line at whether a page serves genuine local user intent independent of its rankings value. Three overlapping policy frameworks apply: (1) the Doorway Abuse spam policy penalizes pages that exist solely to funnel traffic from location-specific queries, specifically calling out city-swapped page sets; (2) the Scaled Content Abuse policy (formalized March 2024) targets mass-produced pages that manipulate rankings without proportional user value, explicitly including programmatic city pages; (3) the Helpful Content / E-E-A-T framework, now baked into core ranking rather than a periodic signal, evaluates whether a page demonstrates genuine local experience and expertise and would satisfy a user who arrived without a search engine. Local search intent for home-service contractors is high-commercial-urgency (46% of all Google searches carry local intent; 76% of local mobile searches produce an offline visit within a day), and users in a specific town expect genuinely town-specific information: local trust signals, area-specific context, and evidence the contractor actually serves that market. Google rewards pages that reflect authentic community connection; it penalizes pages that could pass the "swap test" — where swapping the city name is the only meaningful difference between pages on the same site.
key_findings: Google's Doorway Abuse spam policy (last updated May 2026, continuously enforced) explicitly cites 'multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page' as a primary example of doorway abuse. The defining test: 'Would this page exist if search engines did not?' Source: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies

The March 2024 spam update added Scaled Content Abuse as a named policy: 'generating many pages primarily to manipulate search rankings, with little or no value added for users.' The example pattern it targets is exactly the contractor city-page anti-pattern: copying a template article, swapping a few nouns, and publishing thousands of city-level pages. The rollout reduced low-quality content in results by 45%. Source: https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies

The Helpful Content system was merged into Google's core ranking signals in March 2024, making it a continuous real-time signal rather than a periodic update. A site-wide unhelpfulness signal can suppress even genuinely good pages on the same domain. This means a batch of thin location pages risks pulling down the whole contractor site. Source: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content

E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trust) is Google's framework for evaluating content quality, with Trust as the most important component. For local home-service contractors, Trust is built through: verifiable license/credentials on-page, Google reviews (4.5+ stars correlates with higher local-pack rankings), named technicians/team, and a local business address. Quality Raters treat home service businesses as YMYL-adjacent because a bad hire creates real-world harm risk. Source: https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/12/google-raters-guidelines-e-e-a-t

The 'swap test' is the practitioner's operationalization of doorway detection: place two city pages side by side — if 90%+ of the content is identical with only the city name changed, Google's systems (and human raters) treat it as a doorway campaign. An HVAC company with hundreds of such pages lost 80%+ of their rankings after March 2024. Source: https://ricketyroo.com/blog/location-page-spam/

Local search intent for contractor queries is transactional and urgency-driven: 76% of local mobile searches result in an offline visit within one day (Think with Google). Users expect: a phone number that works in their area, evidence the contractor has actually worked in their town, local social proof (reviews from neighbors), and area-specific context (local weather patterns, building codes, housing stock type). Pages that supply this satisfy intent independent of rankings value. Source: https://www.localfalcon.com/blog/what-is-local-search-intent-and-how-can-you-optimize-for-it

BrightLocal documented a 107% lift in rankings from hyperlocal content on location pages versus generic templated pages. The elements that drove the lift were: local weather/climate context, references to local housing types and neighborhoods, area-specific customer reviews, and service-area maps. These are all programmatically generatable from a structured data layer. Source: https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/location-pages/

Google rewards authentic community connection at a hyperlocal level. Specific contractor wins documented: HVAC contractor targeting Santa Rosa/Petaluma/Windsor gained top-3 map positions after adding localized copy and schema markup per location; roofing client moved from third to first in Brentwood TN after adding 18 reviews and embedding a team video. The ranking driver is not the presence of a location page but the quality signal density on it. Source: https://pushleads.com/local-seo-ranking-factors-2025/

Site Reputation Abuse (policy updated December 2024) is a third risk vector: using third-party or white-label content that exploits the host site's domain authority. If King Maker generates location pages using AI-written content that is not grounded in actual local data or contractor experience, Google may classify it under this policy. The violation trigger is 'published in an attempt to abuse search rankings by taking advantage of the host site's ranking signals.' Source: https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/11/site-reputation-abuse

The people-first self-assessment questions Google publishes (developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) include: Does the content demonstrate first-hand expertise from actually using or visiting the place/service? Would a visitor feel satisfied or would they refine their search? Is the content written for an existing audience that would find it useful if they came directly? For a town-specific contractor page, 'first-hand expertise' means the contractor has actual project history in that town — this is the most powerful differentiator available and is already in the contractor's possession.

## Legitimacy Checklist: Every Per-Town Location Page Must Pass

This checklist maps directly to Google's stated tests. Each item is independently verifiable by a programmatic generator given the right data inputs. Items marked [DATA-LAYER] can be seeded once per town and reused across all trade verticals; items marked [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] require per-contractor input.

---

### TIER 1 — DOORWAY ABUSE GATE (binary pass/fail)
These four tests mirror Google's own doorway policy language. A page that fails any one of these is a doorway page by definition.

| # | Gate | How to test | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The swap test**: Remove the town name from both pages — do they read as meaningfully distinct documents? | A human reader should not be able to infer two different towns after redaction without reading service-area text | Google Spam Policies |
| 2 | **The existence test**: Would this page exist if Google did not exist? Could the contractor show this page to a Cary homeowner and have it feel purpose-built for them? | Ask: does the page contain information a Cary resident would find useful that a Raleigh resident would not? | Google Doorway Blog 2015 |
| 3 | **The funnel test**: Does the page stand as a final destination, or does it exist only to push users to a single generic page? | The page must have its own phone/CTA, not just a redirect to the homepage | Google Spam Policies |
| 4 | **The similarity threshold**: No more than ~50% of the body copy should be shared verbatim across all town pages | Use a diff tool or similarity scorer across the page set | RicketyRoo; Manning Search Marketing |

---

### TIER 2 — SCALED CONTENT ABUSE GATE (March 2024 policy)
These items distinguish programmatic pages with proportional value from mass-produced thin content.

| # | Requirement | Implementation note |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Each page has at least **3 town-specific factual claims** that are not present on other town pages | [DATA-LAYER] Seed: local climate/weather pattern, dominant housing stock type (age, style), commute corridor or county-seat context |
| 6 | At least **1 area-specific customer review or project reference** is present or the page explicitly names a town neighborhood/subdivision served | [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] Pull from GBP reviews filtered by city; or quote a project address (neighborhood, not street) |
| 7 | **No AI hallucination of local facts** — every town-specific claim must trace to a real data source (Census, NOAA weather normals, permit records, contractor's own job history) | Template must enforce a data-validated slot, not a free-text LLM fill |
| 8 | Content volume is **proportional to actual service presence** — do not publish a full-depth page for a town the contractor has never served | [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] Only generate pages for towns inside the contractor's actual service radius; list jobs completed there if possible |

---

### TIER 3 — E-E-A-T / HELPFUL CONTENT SIGNALS
These items determine whether Google's quality systems treat the page as experience-backed versus search-engine-only.

| # | Signal | Implementation note |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | **Named contractor identity on-page**: real name, license number (NC license lookup URL linkable), and photo — not just a generic "our team" reference | [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] One-time setup, appears on every location page via template |
| 10 | **Local trust signals**: at minimum, the contractor's Google review average and count displayed, ideally with 1-3 reviews that mention the town by name | [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] Pull from GBP API or embed widget; filter by city |
| 11 | **Area-specific service context**: at least one of — local building code reference (e.g., NC 2018 Residential Code + county amendment), typical local weather hazard (hailstorms in Wake County, hurricane prep on the coast), or local housing era (post-WWII ranch stock vs. new construction subdivisions) | [DATA-LAYER] Structured per county; reusable across all clients in that county |
| 12 | **Service area map or driving context**: embedded map showing coverage from the contractor's base to the town, or explicit statement of travel distance/time | [DATA-LAYER] Auto-generated from lat/long; shows genuine service commitment |
| 13 | **First-person experience signals**: process description uses "we've installed / repaired / replaced in [Town]" language tied to actual job count where possible, not generic "we serve [Town]" | [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] Job-count input per town (even approximate) differentiates from zero-data templates |

---

### TIER 4 — LOCAL SEARCH INTENT MATCH
These items ensure the page satisfies what a local searcher actually wants, independent of rankings value.

| # | User need | Implementation note |
|---|---|---|
| 14 | **Frictionless contact for high-urgency queries**: click-to-call phone number above the fold, prominently visible on mobile | Template requirement; not content-layer |
| 15 | **Emergency vs. scheduled service distinction**: page addresses both intent types — "need it today" (leak, no heat) and "planning a project" (roof replacement, AC upgrade) | [DATA-LAYER] Urgency-intent section templatable; specific seasonal hazards vary by town latitude/climate zone |
| 16 | **Answers the implicit local qualifying question**: "Do you actually come to [Town]?" — page must explicitly confirm service coverage of the town and nearby neighborhoods | Boilerplate plus a named neighborhood list [DATA-LAYER] |
| 17 | **Pricing transparency or cost context**: local cost range or financing option referenced; users with transactional intent abandon pages with no cost signals | [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] Pricing tier or range; or a "free estimate" CTA with response-time commitment |

---

### TIER 5 — SITE-WIDE HEALTH (protects the whole domain)
Because the Helpful Content signal is site-wide, a cluster of thin pages hurts every page on the domain.

| # | Requirement | Implementation note |
|---|---|---|
| 18 | **Do not publish pages for towns you cannot actually serve**: every page in the location set must represent a real service commitment | Enforce via service-radius geography config; delete any page if the contractor stops serving that area |
| 19 | **Internal linking is hierarchical, not flat**: each town page links to the hub service-area page and to at least one relevant service page; the hub page links back to towns | Prevents the "funnel to one page" pattern Google cites |
| 20 | **Schema markup per page**: LocalBusiness schema with `areaServed` set to the specific town, `address` with contractor's real address, `aggregateRating` from real reviews | [DATA-LAYER] + [CLIENT-SPECIFIC] combination; validates geographic claim to Google's structured data parser |

---

### Quick reference: what Google penalizes vs. rewards

| Google penalizes | Google rewards |
|---|---|
| City name swap as the only difference | Town-specific factual content a local resident would recognize |
| Pages that redirect to a generic destination | Pages that satisfy the query completely, on their own |
| AI hallucination of local "facts" | Data-backed local claims (weather, codes, housing stock) |
| Zero contractor identity signals | Named, licensed contractor with verifiable credentials |
| No reviews or generic reviews | Town-filtered reviews showing real local project history |
| Bulk page generation without service commitment | Pages proportional to actual contractor presence in each town |
| Identical FAQ across all towns | FAQs specific to local concerns (e.g., "Do you pull Wake County permits?") |

| 10 | **Local HOA rules affecting the trade** | **MED** — HOA rules on roofing materials, HVAC condenser placement, fence heights are genuinely local; but HOA databases are not publicly queryable at scale | **No** — no public HOA rules API exists; requires manual research or client input | [NC HOA Laws overview](https://www.hopb.co/north-carolina); individual HOA CC&Rs (not machine-readable) | High editorial value if you can get it; not auto-generatable. ---

## Auto-Generation Architecture Summary

For a King Maker template, the minimum viable auto-generated data spine per town (requiring zero client input) hits Tiers 2-3 and delivers structural uniqueness that supports but does not replace client-input content:

| Auto-Generated Layer | API / Source | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Median year built + housing unit count | Census ACS API | Free (API key) |
| Heating/cooling degree days + annual rainfall | NOAA NCEI API | Free (token) |
| Permit jurisdiction name + link | Hardcoded lookup table (30 NC towns) | One-time manual build |
| Drive time from shop to town center | Google Maps Distance Matrix or OSRM | ~$0.005/request (Google) or free (OSRM) |
| Nearest weather station city name | NOAA station lookup | Free |
| 4-6 subdivision names in town | OpenStreetMap Overpass or manual seed list | Free |

**Client-input slots required for Tier 1 (page cannot pass the swap test without them):**
1. At least 1 completed project photo from that town (with job description)
2. At least 1 review that mentions the town or a local neighborhood

Without those two client-input slots, the page is structurally a template regardless of how many data points are injected, and remains at elevated doorway-page risk under Google's current enforcement posture.

findings.summary: Google's March 2024 spam policy update formally codified "scaled content abuse" as a distinct penalty class, targeting pages generated at volume whose primary purpose is ranking manipulation rather than user value — regardless of whether humans or AI produced them. The line separating legitimate multi-location pSEO from spam abuse is not about volume but about per-page informational value: a page survives if removing the location swap still leaves a page a real visitor would find useful. Real per-location data (completed projects, local building codes, city permit patterns, neighborhood home ages, geo-tagged photos, city-specific reviews) is the single most durable differentiator because it cannot be faked at scale and signals genuine service presence. For a small solo contractor with a 30-town service radius, 20-40 indexed location pages that each carry 30-40% genuinely unique, locally-sourced content signals is the safe operating range; thin outlier towns (no jobs done there yet) should be noindexed or held as drafts until real-work evidence exists to populate them.
key_findings: GOOGLE'S OFFICIAL DEFINITION (March 2024): Scaled content abuse = 'generating many pages primarily to manipulate Search rankings, with little or no value added for users.' Google explicitly states this applies whether content is created by automation, humans, or a combination. Source: developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies

DOORWAY PAGES ARE A SEPARATE BUT OVERLAPPING POLICY: Google's doorway abuse policy targets 'pages created to rank for specific, similar queries' that funnel users to an intermediate page less useful than the destination. The swap test failure (remove city name, same page) is the clearest doorway signal. An HVAC company building hundreds of suburb pages with only minor copy swaps lost 63% organic traffic in 30 days after March 2024. Source: ricketyroo.com/blog/location-page-spam/, gsqi.com December 2024 case studies

THE LINE IN PRACTICE: Volume is NOT the issue. Thousands of high-quality pages with distinct data are not penalized. The penalty threshold is volume WITHOUT proportional value. Sterling Sky's guidance: programmatic 70% shared template + 30% manually-shaped local content is the minimum safe ratio. Google's helpful content system has become increasingly aggressive about 'templatized local content' with no genuine local signals. Source: sterlingsky.ca/how-to-create-unique-and-helpful-service-area-pages

HOW LEGITIMATE MULTI-LOCATION BUSINESSES BUILD PAGES SAFELY (post-March 2024): (1) City-specific completed project photos with geo-tags; (2) City-sourced customer reviews displayed on that city's page; (3) Local building code / permit references unique to that municipality; (4) Neighborhood housing stock data (home age, roof type prevalence, storm exposure history); (5) Local supplier or material availability notes; (6) Service-call radius and typical drive time from the contractor's base; (7) LocalBusiness + ServiceArea schema markup with explicit city/zip coverage. Source: constructionmarketingservices.com, backlinko.com/multi-location-seo, almcorp.com/blog/neighborhood-seo

THE ROLE OF REAL DATA vs LLM-SPUN TEXT: Real per-location data is the durability signal. Examples that pass: actual completed jobs in that city (photos + dates), city permit office links, local building codes, DataForSEO or public-record population/housing data, real customer reviews geolocated to that city. LLM-spun city descriptions that amount to 'Apex NC is a growing suburb...' with no operational evidence constitute exactly the scaled content abuse pattern. The key test: could this specific block of content exist on a competitor's site with only city name changed? If yes, it is thin. Source: guptadeepak.com/the-programmatic-seo-paradox, searchengineland.com/guide/programmatic-seo

MINIMUM UNIQUE CONTENT THRESHOLD: No official percentage exists, but industry consensus from Sterling Sky, ContentAmigo, and Search Engine Land converges on: at minimum 30% of the page must be content that could not be replicated by swapping a city token. The safest pattern for contractors is a data-driven unique block anchored in (a) actual jobs completed in that city, (b) city-specific review excerpts, (c) one local regulatory or environmental detail (permit office, common storm patterns, prevailing roof type). The shared template (service description, brand list, FAQ, pricing range, contact CTA) can fill the remaining 70%. Source: contentamigo.com/articles/how-to-make-unique-service-area-pages, sterlingsky.ca, searchengineland.com/guide/service-area-pages

HOW MANY PAGES IS SAFE FOR A SMALL CONTRACTOR: No hard page-count ceiling exists, but the practical guidance for a service-area business with one physical location and a 30-mile radius is: only create a dedicated indexed page for a town where you have at least one real data signal (a job, a review, a local reference). A 20-40 page footprint built on actual job history is lower risk than 150 pages built on template-plus-city-swap. For towns outside active job history, either hold the page as noindexed/draft or create a combined service-area hub entry (not a standalone page). Source: bippermedia.com/seo/service-area-pages-seo, searchengineland.com/local-seo-sprints-90-day-plan, ewizer.com/seo-for-service-area-businesses

INDEX vs NOINDEX STRATEGY: Index pages where genuine local data exists. Noindex (or exclude entirely) pages that are pure template with only the city token changed. A hybrid approach: publish all 30+ location pages but noindex the ones with no local data yet; as you accumulate jobs and reviews in those towns, swap to indexed. Important caveat from ALM Corp (2025): avoid noindex in original page code for pages you intend to eventually index — use canonical or simply withhold publication. Source: almcorp.com/blog/google-noindex-tag-warning-original-page-code, bippermedia.com/seo/service-area-pages-seo

DECEMBER 2024 SPAM UPDATE CONFIRMED ENFORCEMENT: Glenn Gabe's analysis of the December 2024 spam update documented five case studies including 'Doorway Pages Galore' and 'Scaled Content Abuse with PAA Mining.' Sites penalized shared the pattern: high page volume, content differing only by keyword/city token, no real operational data. Sites that survived had genuine differentiation anchors per page. Source: gsqi.com/marketing-blog/google-december-2024-spam-update-case-studies

PROGRAMMATIC SEO THAT SURVIVES AT REAL SCALE (model examples): Zillow location pages survive because each has real property data, school district maps, crime heat maps, and walk scores. NomadList survives because each city page pulls live cost-of-living, internet speed, and weather data. The contractor equivalent: each town page pulls real completed-job data, geo-tagged photos from that town, reviews from customers in that zip code, and the county permit office URL. The template structure is shared; the data payload is real and unique. Source: seomatic.ai/blog/programmatic-seo-examples, backlinko.com/programmatic-seo
findings.deliverable:
## Rules for Safe Auto-Generation of Per-Town Location Pages

### Rule 1 — The Swap Test is the go/no-go gate
Before publishing any location page, apply the swap test: replace the city name with a different city. If the page still reads as useful and accurate, it is a doorway page. Every indexed page must contain at least one block of content that fails the swap test — i.e., content that is factually specific to that city and cannot be reused elsewhere without being wrong.

### Rule 2 — Real operational data is the only durable differentiator
LLM-generated city descriptions ("Apex NC is a fast-growing suburb with many new homes...") are interchangeable and constitute scaled content abuse. Real data signals that pass Google's quality systems:
- Completed job entries for that city (address area, service type, date, before/after photo)
- Customer reviews from that city's zip codes (sourced from Google Business Profile or third-party review platforms)
- The county/city permit office name and URL (publicly verifiable, specific to that municipality)
- Local housing stock facts: median home age, dominant roof type, common HVAC system vintage — sourced from Census/ACS data or county assessor records, not LLM inference
- Any local weather or environmental signal with a verifiable source (e.g., hail frequency from NOAA data for roofing; freeze-thaw cycle days for HVAC)

### Rule 3 — Template : unique ratio = 70:30 minimum, aim for 50:50
Shared template content (service descriptions, brand list, pricing range, FAQ, contact CTA, schema) can fill up to 70% of the page. The remaining 30% must be the city-specific data payload from Rule 2. For higher-value or more competitive cities (Raleigh, Cary, Durham), push toward 50% unique content. The shared 70% is not a liability if the 30% is genuinely local — it is the efficiency gain of the template model.

### Rule 4 — Only index pages with at least one real data anchor
A page with zero completed jobs, zero local reviews, and no verifiable local reference should not be indexed. Options:
- Hold it as a draft until first job data exists
- Publish with `noindex` until first data anchor is added (then flip to indexed)
- Omit it entirely and rely on the service-area hub page to cover that town until jobs are done there
Do not use noindex as a permanent strategy for pages you intend to eventually rank — it is a staging mechanism only.

### Rule 5 — Minimum page count = towns where you have real job history
For a solo/small contractor with a 30-mile radius, the safe indexed footprint is roughly:
- **10–25 pages**: towns with at least 1–2 completed jobs and 1 real review. This is the immediate buildout.
- **25–40 pages**: towns with partial evidence (job photos but no reviews yet, or strong neighboring-city evidence). Borderline — use 40%+ unique content threshold.
- **40+ pages**: only if each page passes Rule 1 independently. Never inflate page count to capture keyword volume; inflate only when job history and review accumulation justify it.

### Rule 6 — Schema signals are not optional, they are the machine-readable proof layer
Every location page must carry:
- `LocalBusiness` schema with the contractor's NAP
- `ServiceArea` property with explicit city name, county, and zip code
- `areaServed` array on the root domain's organization schema listing all served cities
This schema layer is how Google verifies that location claims correspond to a real business footprint, not keyword targeting. Missing schema on location pages is a gap that city-swap text cannot compensate for.

### Rule 7 — The data pipeline must be a real pipeline, not an LLM prompt
Auto-generation is only safe when the unique-content slot is populated from a real data source, not from an AI writing "unique" copy about a city it has never serviced. The build system architecture must include:
- A job/project database per contractor (even a simple spreadsheet) that feeds city-specific project entries into the page template
- A review-pull mechanism (GBP API or manual sync) that associates reviews with their city
- A static data layer for county permit office URLs and housing stock data (Census ACS table B25035 for median year built, per county)
- A flag or quality gate: if a city row in the data layer has zero job entries and zero reviews, the page is not published indexed

### Rule 8 — Pages must stand alone as destinations, not as funnels
Google's doorway abuse policy specifically targets pages that "funnel visitors into the actual usable portion of the site." Each location page must be a complete, useful destination in itself — full contact form or click-to-call, service detail relevant to that city, social proof from that city. If the page's only purpose is to rank for "[service] in [city]" and then push the visitor to the homepage or a generic contact page, it is a doorway page regardless of how much unique text it contains.

### Rule 9 — The shared FAQ must not be the only content differentiation strategy
FAQs are easy to vary by city ("How much does a roof replacement cost in Cary NC?") but city-specific FAQ answers generated by LLM without local pricing data are exactly the pattern Google's SpamBrain targets. If FAQ variation is used, answers must reference real local variables: actual material costs from local supplier data, actual permit fees from the city's fee schedule, actual timeline based on contractor's job history in that market.

### Rule 10 — Build the footprint incrementally, not all at once
Launching 40 identical-except-for-city pages on the same day is a pattern consistent with scaled content abuse and is more likely to trigger SpamBrain review. The safe build sequence:
1. Launch the top 8–12 cities first (highest job density, strongest review concentration)
2. Add remaining cities in batches of 5–8 as job and review data accumulates
3. Monitor Search Console for manual action notices or crawl anomalies after each batch
4. Never launch a new city page until its data payload (Rule 2) is ready

findings.summary: Real-world evidence from 2022-2025 confirms a consistent, well-documented pattern: contractor and home-service sites with per-town pages that rank safely share one structural trait — each page contains content that cannot survive a simple city-name swap. Losers built pages where swapping one string would produce an identical page. Google has targeted this pattern in at least five major spam updates (Oct 2022, Mar 2024, Dec 2024, Aug 2025), through both algorithmic demotion and manual action. The winning playbook concentrates on fewer cities (15-20 max), uses real job documentation (photos, geo-tagged check-ins, named reviews), adds locally specific context (housing stock, climate, building codes), and treats each page as a genuine local resource rather than a ranked template. Google's own John Mueller stated explicitly that 1,300 city pages would be doorway pages, and that swapping a city name plus a few pictures does not constitute unique content.
key_findings: Google's official spam policy (developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) defines doorway abuse as pages 'created to rank for specific, similar search queries' — its own test example is service pages for every city combination that funnel to one page. The same policy added scaled content abuse in March 2024, targeting large volumes of pages where city-name substitution produces functionally identical pages.

October 2022 spam update (Search Engine Land) hit service-area business (SAB) sites hardest, with the mechanism being automatic DEINDEXING of duplicate location pages rather than a ranking demotion. Sites lost individual URLs from the index, collapsing rankings for those city-service queries. The common thread: copy written for search engines, not humans — passing only the city name through a template.

March 2024 core update + spam update documented case (Search Engine Land / Content Ladder): a regional HVAC company with hundreds of suburb pages (minor copy swaps only) saw 80%+ of those pages lose rankings, with a 63% organic traffic drop in 30 days. Recovery required consolidating to comprehensive location pages with real unique content and per-city customer reviews.

Google December 2024 spam update (gsqi.com, 5 case studies by Glenn Gabe): a site with large volumes of doorway-style location pages combined with AI-generated content crammed at the bottom of each page was penalized heavily. Specific signals: 100% AI-generation probability on the bottom-of-page copy blocks, off-topic content, every PAA turned into a heading. Outcome: big ranking drop, no fast recovery path.

Google August 2025 spam update continued enforcement on near-identical location pages. Multiple analyses (localdominator.co, infintechdesigns.com, sterlingsky.ca) confirm that HVAC/contractor sites running dozens of pages differing only in city name were demoted. Sterling Sky's case study noted the update also unraveled spammy exact-match backlink anchor text built years earlier, compounding losses.

John Mueller (Google Search Advocate) stated directly (localsearchforum.com thread, seroundtable.com coverage): 1,300 city-based landing pages targeting [keyword + city] are doorway pages against Google guidelines. He also stated: 'You can't swap out the city name or a few pictures and then call it good. These local landing pages with duplicated content can be considered doorway pages.'

BrightLocal's authoritative guide to location pages identifies the single differentiator: 'content with unique value — saying the same thing with different words doesn't make content more valuable, it's essentially duplicated.' Their required unique elements: driving directions specific to that office/service area, nearby landmarks, local housing or climate context, per-city reviews, and local project case studies.

Plumbing Webmasters (a plumber-specialist SEO agency with 1,000+ campaigns) recommends a strict 15 city page maximum, with each page requiring real job documentation from that city — no scraped content, no gibberish. They found that authentic job-documentation pages (photos + descriptions of work done in that city) are 'perfectly within Google's guidelines and will rank.'

DataPins (a widely-used local SEO tool for HVAC/plumbing) solves the uniqueness problem programmatically: technicians check in at each jobsite, generating a geo-tagged 'pin' with real photos, job description, and schema markup that auto-publishes to the corresponding city page. This makes each page's content literally irreproducible by competitors — it comes from work only that company performed in that location.

The 70/30 rule from current SEO practice (arc4.com, revved.digital): the best programmatic city pages automate 70% of structure/boilerplate and allow 30% to be manually shaped or dynamically filled with location-unique signals (local reviews, job photos, climate/housing notes, landmarks). Google's John Mueller's implicit threshold: if removing the city name and inserting another would produce a fully functional page, it is a doorway page.

findings.summary: Dedicated per-town location pages can be safely re-introduced for King Maker contractor sites if each page clears the "swap test" with genuinely town-specific content layered on top of shared structural scaffolding — targeting 80-90% unique content per page. The core risk vectors are Google's Doorway Abuse policy (pages that only swap a city name), Scaled Content Abuse (volume without proportional value, effective May 5 2024), and the residual signal confusion from the previous 308 redirects that pointed /locations/{town} → /service-area#{town}. A hub-and-spoke URL structure with a /service-area hub and /locations/{town} spokes, combined with correct LocalBusiness + Service schema using areaServed (not the deprecated serviceArea), a governed sitemap that only lists ready pages, and a hard content-minimum gate before any spoke goes live, gives the highest likelihood of safe indexation. key_findings: Google's Doorway Abuse policy (developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) explicitly cites 'multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page' as the canonical violation. The swap test — 'if you swap the city name does the page become identical?' — is the practical threshold.

Google's Scaled Content Abuse policy (effective May 5 2024, per developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies) targets pages generated primarily to manipulate rankings rather than help users, regardless of whether automation or humans created them. Volume without proportional value is the trigger, not automation per se.

The March 2024 Core Update and December 2024 Spam Update both aggressively targeted city-swap location pages. Case studies show 80%+ ranking loss and 63% organic traffic drop in 30 days for HVAC/home-service sites that had hundreds of near-identical suburb pages (documented in GSQI December 2024 Spam Update case studies).

Sterling Sky's authoritative service-area-pages guide (sterlingsky.ca/how-to-create-unique-and-helpful-service-area-pages) and BrightLocal both confirm that city-specific reviews, job photos taken in that town, local landmark references, and town-specific cost/permit data are the highest-ROI uniqueness signals — and they are programmatically generatable from a structured data layer.

schema.org/areaServed has superseded the deprecated serviceArea property. The correct pattern for a service-area contractor (no storefront in serviced towns) is: root LocalBusiness node on the homepage with areaServed listing all towns + a per-page Service node on each spoke with areaServed scoped to that single town. Do NOT add a separate LocalBusiness node on spoke pages — that creates phantom multi-location signals.

The physical-address / service-area distinction is a real doorway risk factor: Google Business Profile guidelines explicitly say SABs should hide their address. On the schema side, do not embed a full PostalAddress for a town where the contractor has no office — use areaServed with an AdministrativeArea or City entity instead.

Reversing a 308 (permanent) redirect is technically safe but carries a 4-8 week equity reconsolidation lag. Google treated the 308 as a canonical signal pointing to /service-area#{town}. When you restore /locations/{town}, Googlebot must re-discover the page, re-evaluate canonical, and re-associate any backlink equity. During this window the spoke page may rank weakly. Mitigation: restore redirects in batches of 5-10 towns per week, prioritize highest-revenue towns first, and verify re-indexation in Search Console before the next batch.

Hub-and-spoke is the correct URL architecture: /service-area (hub, canonical, keeps any existing backlinks to the consolidated page) + /locations/{town-slug} (spokes). Do NOT create a flat /raleigh-hvac structure — the nested path signals the geographic sub-taxonomy to crawlers and keeps link equity flowing hub→spoke→hub via reciprocal internal links.

Crawl budget and sitemap governance: include a spoke URL in sitemap.xml ONLY after it meets the content minimum gate. Pages that are live but below the gate should return 200 with a noindex meta tag temporarily — NOT be excluded from crawl via robots.txt (which would prevent Google from reading the noindex). Remove noindex and add to sitemap only when content is ready.

For towns with little real data (population under 15,000, fewer than 3 completed jobs there): do NOT create a spoke page. Keep them as anchor links on the /service-area hub with a schema areaServed entry. Creating a spoke for a town with nothing town-specific to say is the definition of scaled content abuse.

## Technical Architecture Spec: Per-Town Location Pages for King Maker Contractor Sites

---

### 1. URL Structure — Hub-and-Spoke, Not Flat

**Structure**

```
/service-area                          ← hub (keep, existing backlinks live here)
/locations/raleigh                     ← spoke
/locations/cary
/locations/apex
/locations/wake-forest
...
```

**Rationale**

The `/locations/{town-slug}` nested path signals geographic sub-taxonomy to crawlers and makes the parent-child relationship explicit. A flat `/raleigh-hvac` pattern loses that signal and creates slug collisions across multi-trade clients. The hub stays live and retains any equity that accumulated on `/service-area` during the consolidation period — do not delete or redirect it.

**Slug rules**
- Lowercase, hyphenated, NC town name only: `/locations/wake-forest` not `/locations/wake-forest-hvac-nc`
- No trailing slash inconsistency — pick one and enforce it sitewide via canonical
- Canonical tag on each spoke: `<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/locations/raleigh" />`

---

### 2. Schema — LocalBusiness + Service + areaServed

**Root node (homepage only)**

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "HomeAndConstructionBusiness",
  "name": "Acme Roofing",
  "url": "https://example.com",
  "telephone": "+1-919-555-0100",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "123 Main St",
    "addressLocality": "Raleigh",
    "addressRegion": "NC",
    "postalCode": "27601",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "areaServed": [
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Raleigh", "sameAs": "https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q179263"},
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Cary"},
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Apex"},
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Wake Forest"}
  ]
}
```

**Per-spoke node (on each /locations/{town} page)**

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Service",
  "name": "Roof Replacement in Cary NC",
  "serviceType": "Roof Replacement",
  "provider": {
    "@type": "HomeAndConstructionBusiness",
    "name": "Acme Roofing",
    "url": "https://example.com"
  },
  "areaServed": {
    "@type": "City",
    "name": "Cary",
    "containedInPlace": {
      "@type": "State",
      "name": "North Carolina"
    }
  },
  "description": "Licensed roof replacement serving Cary homeowners..."
}
```

**Critical rules**
- Do NOT add a second full `LocalBusiness` node on spoke pages — it creates phantom multi-location signals that confuse GBP and may trigger the physical-address doorway risk.
- Use `areaServed` (current). The `serviceArea` property is deprecated as of Schema.org v7+.
- Do NOT embed a `PostalAddress` for a town where the contractor has no physical office.
- Use the most specific `@type` subclass available: `RoofingContractor`, `HVACBusiness`, `Plumber`, `Electrician` — not generic `LocalBusiness`.

---

### 3. Internal Linking — Reinforce, Not Cannibalize

**Hub → Spokes**
The `/service-area` hub links to every active spoke via a service-area map/grid component. Anchor text pattern: "Roofing in {Town}" (keyword + city, not bare city name).

**Spoke → Hub**
Every spoke links back to the hub with text like "See our full {Trade} service area →". This reciprocal link is what prevents spoke pages from becoming isolated doorway-style dead ends.

**Spoke → Spoke**
Link to 2-3 geographically adjacent towns only. Do not create a full cross-link matrix — that dilutes equity and looks manipulative. Adjacency rule: towns within 10 miles or part of the same county.

**Service pages → Spokes**
The `/services/roof-replacement` page includes a "Cities We Serve" section linking to 4-6 highest-volume spoke pages. This creates cross-dimensional links (service → location) that strengthen topical authority.

**Canonicalization discipline**
Each spoke has exactly one canonical URL. If the same content is reachable via `/locations/raleigh` and `/locations/raleigh-nc`, one must 301 to the other — no exceptions.

---

### 4. Reversing the 308 Redirects — Analysis and Protocol

**What happened:** `/locations/{town}` → 308 → `/service-area#{town}`
Google treated these 308s as permanent canonical signals. Link equity and crawl priority were consolidated to `/service-area`. The spoke URLs were effectively dropped from the index.

**What reversal means for equity**
When you restore `/locations/{town}` and remove the 308, Googlebot must:
1. Re-crawl the restored URL
2. Re-evaluate canonical (the page now exists, no redirect)
3. Re-associate any inbound links that pointed to the old spoke URLs
4. De-consolidate from `/service-area`

This process takes **4-8 weeks** and may cause a temporary ranking dip on both the hub and the new spoke during re-consolidation. This is expected and recoverable.

**Reversal protocol (batched)**

| Week | Action |
|------|--------|
| 0 | Verify content for top 5 revenue towns meets minimum gate (see §6) |
| 1 | Remove 308s for those 5 towns, restore /locations/{town}, add to sitemap, submit to Search Console via URL Inspection |
| 2-3 | Monitor Search Console Coverage + Performance for those 5 URLs |
| 4 | If indexing confirmed, proceed to next batch of 5-10 towns |
| Ongoing | Do not restore a spoke redirect until that town's page meets content gate |

**Towns not ready:** Leave 308 in place OR return 404 (Google treats 404 as "no longer exists" which is honest). Do not return a 200 with thin content — that is worse than a redirect.

---

### 5. Sitemap + Indexation Governance

**Rule: sitemap is a quality signal, not an inventory export**

Only include spoke URLs that have passed the content minimum gate. Including thin pages in sitemap signals to Google that you consider them canonical and worth indexing — it does not protect you, it flags you.

**Sitemap structure**

```xml
<!-- sitemap-index.xml -->
<sitemapindex>
  <sitemap><loc>/sitemap-core.xml</loc></sitemap>
  <sitemap><loc>/sitemap-locations.xml</loc></sitemap>
</sitemapindex>
```

Separate the locations sitemap so you can submit/resubmit it independently in Search Console without re-crawling the entire site.

**Staging a spoke page**
1. Page is built but below content gate → serve 200 + `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">` + exclude from sitemap
2. Content gate passed → remove noindex tag + add URL to sitemap-locations.xml + submit in Search Console
3. Never block via robots.txt — that prevents Google from reading the noindex directive

**lastmod discipline**
Set `<lastmod>` to the date of meaningful content changes only. Do not auto-update `lastmod` on every deploy — Google penalizes sitemap inflation.

---

### 6. Content Minimum Gate — The Doorway Line

A spoke page MUST contain ALL of the following before going live (no noindex, in sitemap):

| Element | Minimum requirement | Programmatic source |
|---------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Town-specific H1 | "{Trade} in {Town}, NC" — not duplicated across spokes | `lib/data.ts` → `LOCATIONS` |
| Unique opening paragraph | 80+ words that would fail the swap test | `lib/content-home.ts` → `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].intro` — must vary meaningfully |
| Local social proof | ≥1 review or testimonial geo-tagged to that town | Pull from GBP API or CRM jobs data |
| Local landmark / neighborhood reference | ≥1 specific named reference (park, subdivision, school district, major road) | `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].landmarks` array |
| Town-specific FAQ entry | ≥1 FAQ that is specific to that town's conditions (permit office, HOA prevalence, common weather issue) | `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].faq` array |
| Job count or proof of work | "We've completed X+ roofing projects in {Town}" or photo of a local job | CRM data or `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].jobCount` |
| Service schema | Per-spoke Service schema (see §2) | Auto-generated from `lib/data.ts` |
| Internal link to hub | "See our full service area →" | Template component |

**Towns with insufficient data (population < 15,000 or < 3 completed jobs)**
Do NOT create a spoke page. Add the town as an `areaServed` entry in root schema and an anchor on the `/service-area` hub only. Building a spoke page for a town where you have nothing specific to say is textbook scaled content abuse.

---

### 7. Guardrail List

**Hard stops — if any of these are true, do not publish the spoke:**

- [ ] All unique content fields in `LOCATION_CONTENT[town]` are empty or contain only template defaults
- [ ] The page body passes the swap test (remove city name, it reads identically to another spoke)
- [ ] No geo-tagged social proof exists for that town
- [ ] The 308 redirect to `/service-area` has not been explicitly removed and the new URL confirmed returning 200
- [ ] The URL is already indexed as a canonical variant of `/service-area` and the redirect has been live less than 4 weeks (wait for re-consolidation)

**Ongoing quality guardrails:**

- [ ] Run a quarterly swap test across all live spokes — if two pages score >70% similarity on a diff, merge or differentiate
- [ ] Add new towns only after CRM confirms ≥3 completed jobs there (proof of real service, not speculation)
- [ ] Never auto-populate `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].intro` with only city-name substitutions — require at least one field that references a verifiable local data point
- [ ] Do not exceed 30 spoke pages per contractor site without a content audit — quality beats quantity, and 15-20 high-quality spokes outperform 100 thin ones
- [ ] Monitor Google Search Console Coverage weekly for the first 60 days after redirect reversal — "Crawled - currently not indexed" on spokes is a signal to improve content, not to re-submit
- [ ] Do not use the same `Service` schema `description` value across multiple spokes — it is machine-readable duplicate content
