verdicts.assessment:
The proposed recipe is substantially stronger than the deleted doorway pages and would survive casual enforcement. But several components are structurally misleading about their actual uniqueness value, and the framing contains optimism that a Google spam reviewer would not share. Here is the honest breakdown.

WHAT HOLDS UP UNDER ADVERSARIAL REVIEW

Components 1 and 2 (completed local projects + local reviews) are the only components that fully pass the swap test by construction. A photo of a roof replacement on Creekwood Drive in Apex with a date and job description cannot be reused in Cary. A review that says "they were at my house in Wakefield Plantation within two hours" cannot be reused in Holly Springs. These are the bedrock. Everything else is supporting material, not a substitute.

Component 3 (Census ACS housing stock data) is genuinely place-bound — the median year built for Apex homes (B25035_001E at GEOID level) is a different number than for Cary or Fuquay-Varina. It passes the swap test as a data point. The concern is how it is rendered: "67% of Apex homes were built before 2000 — aging HVAC systems are the #1 service call here" is a sentence an LLM writes from the data. That sentence, absent the underlying data citation, looks identical to LLM city-description boilerplate. The safe implementation shows the actual Census figure inline — "Apex: median home built 1999 (US Census ACS 2022)" — so the data is machine-verifiable, not just asserted.

Components 4 through 7 (permit jurisdiction, climate data, subdivision names, drive time) are structurally sound because they reference externally verifiable, location-specific facts. The permit jurisdiction for Cary is issued by the Town, not Wake County — that sentence fails the swap test because it is wrong if you substitute Durham. Drive time from a Raleigh shop to Apex is a different number than drive time to Wake Forest. NOAA HDD/CDD values per weather station differ per town. These hold.

WHAT FAILS THE ADVERSARIAL TEST

Component 8 (local pricing context) is the weakest auto-generated component. "Raleigh-area labor rates run ~8% above the NC state average" is drawn from RSMeans/BLS data at a metro level, not a town level. Apex, Cary, Holly Springs, and Morrisville are all in the Raleigh MSA — they get the identical sentence. The only token that changes is the city name prepended to it. This is definitionally a doorway pattern: the content is true regardless of which Raleigh suburb you name. It fails the swap test within the metro. Flag this as thin unless it is indexed only at the MSA level on one page, not replicated per suburb.

Component 9 (local landmarks / geography references) is explicitly acknowledged as supporting texture in the recipe, but the honest assessment is worse than that: Google's spam systems specifically pattern-match "near Jordan Lake" / "off Highway 55 in Apex" constructions because they appear in tens of millions of LLM-generated city pages from 2023–2024. A single landmark reference is not a uniqueness signal — it is a boilerplate tell. If the rest of the page is data-driven and has a real project photo, one landmark sentence is harmless noise. If it is one of only three "unique" elements on the page, it is negative signal.

Component 10 (local HOA rules) is correctly flagged as non-auto-generatable, but the proposed workaround — "a 'common HOA rules in [town]' section that names specific active HOAs (verifiable)" — is still problematic. Naming Wakefield Plantation HOA and stating its roof-material rules requires knowing those rules. If they are written from LLM inference ("most HOAs in Apex require architectural shingles"), that sentence passes the swap test for any suburb — it is generic. If you cannot link to the actual CC&R document or HOA contact, this component adds legal liability exposure without meaningfully passing the swap test.

Component 12 (local demographics / population context) as written in the recipe is explicitly "LOW-MED" and the recipe's own note is correct — it should be used only as secondary data. The adversarial concern is that population context is exactly what low-effort city-page generators produced en masse before the March 2024 update. "Apex has 65,000 residents" is indistinguishable from those pages. Do not use it at all as a standalone component.

THE CRITICAL MISSING PIECE THE RECIPE UNDERWEIGHTS

The recipe's "two client-input slots" framing — one project photo + one review — is stated as the threshold between template and unique page. That framing is too lenient. One geo-tagged photo and one review keep the page off the worst-offender list, but they do not make a page genuinely useful enough to justify a unique URL under Google's March 2024 helpful-content standard. The standard is not "is any unique content present" — it is "would a real visitor in that city find this page more useful than the service-area hub?" For thin towns (one job three years ago, one review), the honest answer is no, and a spam reviewer looking at 30 nearly-identical pages will apply that standard.

The recipe also does not address the AI-text fingerprint problem. A page where the data spine is real (Census figures, NOAA numbers, permit office URL) but all the prose surrounding it is LLM-written will still read as AI-generated text to Google's content classifiers. Google's March 2024 update did not ban AI text — it banned AI text that exists primarily for ranking. The distinguishing signal is whether the prose reflects genuine operational experience. "We replaced 34 roofs in Apex in 2024, mostly in Haddon Hall and Regency Park subdivisions, where 1990s architectural shingles are failing at the 30-year mark" is operator-authored experience. "Apex NC homeowners face unique roofing challenges due to the area's climate and housing stock" is AI boilerplate. The recipe needs to enforce the former pattern, not just inject data tokens into the latter.

THE SCHEMA CLAIM IS CORRECT BUT INCOMPLETE

Rule 6 (schema markup) is right that LocalBusiness + ServiceArea schema is non-optional. What the recipe misses is that schema alone cannot compensate for thin page content — Google's documentation explicitly states that structured data is not a ranking signal when the page it decorates fails quality filters. Schema is the machine-readable proof layer, but the human-readable content must pass first.

RULE 10 (INCREMENTAL BUILD) IS THE STRONGEST PRACTICAL RULE

Launching 8–12 high-job-density towns first is correct both for Google compliance and for the real-data constraint. A contractor who has done 40 jobs in Cary, 15 in Apex, and zero in Zebulon should have indexed pages for Cary and Apex but not for Zebulon. The job-history database is not just a nice-to-have SEO feature — it is the constraint that makes the whole architecture honest. Without enforcement of this rule, the 10-step recipe degrades into a sophisticated-looking doorway system.
components_that_fail: Component 8 (local pricing context at metro/MSA granularity): Raleigh MSA labor-rate sentences are identical across Apex, Cary, Holly Springs, Morrisville, and Garner — only the city name token changes. This is definitionally a doorway pattern within the metro cluster. It fails the swap test across suburbs.

Component 12 (local demographics / population context): 'Apex has 65,000 residents' is the canonical example of LLM city-page boilerplate that the March 2024 update targeted. Population count without trade-relevant framing adds no user value and is a negative signal because it matches the mass-generated city-page fingerprint.

Component 9 (local landmarks / geography references) when used as a primary uniqueness carrier: 'near Jordan Lake' / 'off Highway 55 in Apex' constructions are pattern-matched by SpamBrain as boilerplate because they appear in tens of millions of 2023-2024 AI city pages. Safe only as one sentence of texture on a page with strong Tier 1 content — not as a standalone differentiator.

Component 10 (HOA rules) implemented via LLM inference: 'Most HOAs in Apex require architectural shingles' passes the swap test for any NC suburb. Without a link to a specific HOA's actual CC&R document, this component is asserting generic knowledge as local knowledge — exactly the scaled-content-abuse pattern.

Any component where the Census/NOAA data is injected into LLM-written prose without the raw figure cited: 'Apex homeowners face unique HVAC challenges due to the area's climate and aging housing stock' is AI boilerplate regardless of whether the author looked up the Census median-year-built figure. The data must appear as a cited number, not just inform the prose.
whats_missing: A prose-authenticity enforcement rule: the recipe specifies what data to inject but not how the prose around the data must be written. There is a hard distinction between operator-authored experience prose ('we replaced 34 roofs in Apex in 2024, mostly in Haddon Hall') and data-spine-plus-LLM-wrap prose. The recipe needs an explicit rule that the connecting copy must be either operator-authored or read-back from verified job records — not LLM-generated text that mentions the data.

A per-town indexing gate tied to job-count minimums: the recipe says 'at least one real data anchor' but does not specify a floor. One job from 2019 with no recent reviews is not a sufficient anchor for a town that is otherwise template-only. A defensible gate is: minimum 2 completed jobs within 24 months OR minimum 3 reviews tagged to that town within 18 months.

An explicit anti-MSA-collapse rule: the recipe does not address the within-metro problem. When 8 suburban towns share the same MSA labor rates, the same nearest NOAA station, and the same permit-fee ranges, the only differentiators remaining are housing-stock figures (which differ meaningfully at the place level), completed jobs, and reviews. The recipe should acknowledge that Tier 2 components 4-8 often collapse to identical values across nearby suburbs and that Tier 1 client-input content becomes the primary load-bearer for same-metro pages.

A content-age / data-freshness policy: Census ACS data used on a page should be labeled with its vintage year. NOAA climate normals should cite the 1991-2020 normals period. A page using 2015 Census estimates in 2026 is presenting stale data as current local fact — which is a quality signal failure independent of the doorway question.

A page-length floor tied to unique-content density: the recipe sets a 30% unique-content ratio but does not specify minimum page length. A 400-word page that is 30% unique contains 120 words of unique content. A 1,200-word page at 30% contains 360 words. Google's quality thresholds are not percentage-based in isolation — absolute informational depth matters. The recipe should specify a minimum unique-content word count (suggested: 300+ words of genuinely town-specific content per indexed page).
verdicts.zero_percent_reality:
A literal 0% chance of doorway-page penalty is not achievable and should not be promised to the client. Here is the honest framing.

The enforcement risk is a spectrum, not a binary. Google's SpamBrain operates on probability scoring across a site's entire page set, not page-by-page manual review. A site with 30 location pages where each has a verified project photo, a tagged review, and real Census/NOAA data will score very differently from a site with 30 pages that share 90% identical prose with only city-name tokens changed. The former is not zero-risk — it is low-risk, and the practical ceiling is "unlikely to trigger automated enforcement, resilient to a manual review."

The honest target to frame for a client is: "built to survive a manual spam review" — meaning a Google quality rater looking at the page set could not reasonably conclude the pages exist primarily to rank for [trade] [city] queries rather than to serve real visitors in those cities. That standard is achievable with the recipe as corrected: Tier 1 client-input content (project photos + tagged reviews) as the non-negotiable foundation, Tier 2 auto-generated data spine as supporting structure, and a hard no-index gate for towns with no job history.

What cannot be zeroed out: (1) the risk that Google's systems weigh the shared template structure across all 30 pages more heavily than the unique-content payload, particularly in the first 6-12 months before a link and review profile develops; (2) the risk that a competitor manually reports the site under the spam policy (this triggers human review regardless of quality); (3) the risk that a future Google algorithm update reweights uniqueness signals in a way that retroactively penalizes pages that met the 2024-2026 standard. These risks are not managed by content quality alone — they require the site to accumulate genuine authority signals (GBP reviews, backlinks, citation consistency) that make the location pages credible on factors beyond the page text.

verdicts.assessment:
## Adversarial Stress-Test: Per-Town Location Page Uniqueness Recipe

The recipe is well-researched and contains genuinely defensible components, but it also contains several components that — when auto-generated without real local data — recreate the exact doorway pattern they are trying to escape. Here is a component-by-component verdict, ordered from most to least defensible.

---

### Components that are genuinely defensible

**Completed local projects with geo-tagged photos (Tier 1, #1)**
Verdict: This is the only component that is structurally undefeatable. A job photo with EXIF geodata, a street-level address reference, and a before/after description is inherently place-bound and cannot be LLM-spun. The March 2026 core update case language from Scorpion.co makes this explicit: "pages that say you serviced 47 homes in a specific neighborhood, show photos of real trucks in real driveways beat 200 templated landing pages." No adversarial objection here — this component is the anchor. The critical weakness is that the recipe correctly marks it as non-auto-generatable, meaning it only protects pages that actually have it. Pages published without it are naked templates regardless of the data spine volume.

**Town-specific customer reviews mentioning the town (Tier 1, #2)**
Verdict: Genuinely defensible when sourced from real reviewers. The GBP API does expose review text. The adversarial problem is the extraction filter: the recipe proposes filtering reviews where "the reviewer mentions a neighborhood or subdivision." In practice, most Google reviews from small contractors are one-line ratings with no location detail. The usable subset is small and will be zero for many towns early in the business's life. A page that shows one review saying "great job on my roof" with no town mention is not materially different from a page with no reviews at all — it is still a template. The recipe acknowledges this but understates how empty the client-input slots will be at launch for the majority of towns.

**Town-specific permit jurisdiction + pull requirements (Tier 2, #4)**
Verdict: The jurisdiction identity — "in Cary, roofing permits are issued by the Town, not Wake County, and inspections happen within 3 business days" — is the strongest auto-generatable uniqueness signal in the recipe. It is verifiable, useful, legally relevant to homeowners, and cannot be replicated for a different city by swapping a token. The adversarial risk is that this component requires a maintained lookup table: fee schedules change, jurisdictions merge, and an outdated permit claim is worse than no claim (it is incorrect and discoverable). The recipe marks it as "partial" auto-generatable, which is accurate. For North Carolina's 30-town service radius this is buildable as a static seed table — but it is a one-time manual build that degrades without maintenance.

---

### Components that are defensible but weaker than claimed

**Housing-stock data from Census ACS (Tier 1, #3)**
Verdict: The data is real and auto-generatable. The adversarial concern is specificity dilution: ACS 5-year estimates at the "place" level (e.g., "Apex town, NC") are accurate and verifiable. However, for small towns or rural areas where Census reports at the county or ZCTA level rather than the place level, the data becomes county-wide — the same number appears on every town page within that county. That means "67% of homes in Johnston County were built before 2000" is shared verbatim across Smithfield, Selma, Four Oaks, and Clayton pages, which reinstates the token-swap problem at the county grain. The recipe does not address this degradation. Additionally, the specific framing ("67% of Apex homes were built before 2000") requires converting ACS vintage distribution tables into a percentage, which is non-trivial and error-prone if done naively. The data is real; the template copy it generates can still sound identical across neighboring towns if they share a county-level data source.

**Climate / weather data from NOAA (Tier 2, #5)**
Verdict: This is the component most at risk of being dismissed as boilerplate-with-numbers swapped. The specific problem is geographic resolution: NOAA degree-day data is collected at weather station level, and the station closest to Apex NC may be the same station used for Cary, Holly Springs, and Fuquay-Varina. The NOAA CPC documentation confirms that degree-day statistics for a given city are often drawn from a single airport station (RDU in this case) with a radius that covers the entire Raleigh-Cary metro. All four location pages would then share identical HDD/CDD numbers, making the copy interchangeable. The recipe's example — "Apex averages 3,820 heating degree-days per year — your furnace works harder here than in Charlotte" — is true, but "Cary averages 3,820 heating degree-days per year" would be equally true and equally generated. Google's systems, which compare pages across a site at crawl time, will detect that this block is numerically identical across nearby-town pages. NOAA climate data is a supporting texture component, not a primary uniqueness carrier, for towns within the same metro.

**Neighborhood / subdivision names (Tier 2, #6)**
Verdict: The concept is sound — naming Wakefield, Brier Creek, Lochmere is locally resonant and passes the swap test. The auto-generation risk is significant: OpenStreetMap's neighbourhood tags are inconsistently populated and have documented reliability issues (the search results confirm an open-edit model where anyone can alter data, with known manipulation incidents). Auto-generating subdivision lists from OSM without manual review will produce errors — wrong names, misspelled subdivisions, or in some cases, fabricated entries. A page that names a subdivision that does not exist in the claimed town is a trust-negative signal and a potential E-E-A-T liability, not an asset. The recipe should require manual verification of the seed list rather than trusting OSM output directly. Sterling Sky's research identifies this lever as high-performing specifically when the names are accurate and local — the adversarial risk is that auto-population without verification will introduce inaccuracies that undermine the page's credibility.

**Drive time from shop (Tier 2, #7)**
Verdict: Technically auto-generatable and genuinely unique per town. The adversarial concern is that this is a one-sentence signal: "We're 14 minutes from downtown Apex." That sentence takes up approximately 12 words on a page. Eleven similar sentences across eleven nearby-town pages — each differing only in a number and a town name — look exactly like token-swap content when Google evaluates the structural similarity of pages across a domain. Drive time is a valid texture signal but has zero weight as a primary uniqueness carrier. The recipe correctly places this in Tier 2 but overstates its uniqueness leverage.

**Local pricing context (Tier 2, #8)**
Verdict: This is the weakest auto-generatable component in the recipe. The adversarial case is severe: RSMeans and 4BT location cost factors operate at the metro or county level, not the town level. "Raleigh-area labor rates run 8% above the NC state average" applies identically to Cary, Apex, Holly Springs, and every other Raleigh-metro town. Every page in a 30-mile radius will carry the same pricing sentence. This is not uniqueness — it is a regional statistic applied as if it were local, which is exactly the kind of nominal localization that Google's scaled-content-abuse policy targets. The 4BT documentation itself states that nationally-averaged location factors are not reliable for high-quality estimates and do not account for local codes, productivity, or permit fees. Using these numbers for marketing copy while implying local specificity is also a credibility risk if a savvy homeowner challenges the framing. This component should be removed from the "auto-generatable" category entirely and replaced with actual job-pricing data from the contractor's own CRM.

---

### Components that are supporting texture only (correctly tiered)

**Local landmarks / geography references (Tier 3, #9):** One or two sentences; valid texture. Not a primary differentiator. The adversarial note is that generating these from OpenStreetMap POI queries can produce obviously mechanical output ("located near Jordan Lake, Highway 55, and the Beaver Creek Commons shopping center") that reads as templated. Hand-written local flavor beats auto-generated POI lists.

**HOA rules (Tier 3, #10):** No scalable data source exists. The recipe correctly marks this non-auto-generatable. Do not attempt to fabricate or generalize HOA content — this is a defamation and accuracy risk if you name specific HOAs and get the rules wrong.

**Local crew members (Tier 3, #11):** Correctly marked as requiring client input. This is a strong E-E-A-T signal but not a template feature.

**Population/demographics (Tier 3, #12):** Correctly marked as low-value. "Apex has 65,000 residents" does not help a homeowner decide on a roofing contractor and Google knows it.

---

### What the safe-pSEO rules get right and where they fail

Rules 1-3 (swap test, real operational data, 70:30 ratio) are correct and well-grounded in current enforcement evidence. The March 2026 core update data confirms that templated city pages were still being penalized as recently as April 2026, meaning this is an ongoing enforcement posture, not a one-time event.

Rule 4 (only index pages with at least one real data anchor) is the most important operational rule and the one most likely to be violated in practice. The recipe's proposed auto-generated data spine — Census housing data, NOAA climate data, drive time, subdivision names, permit jurisdiction — is NOT sufficient to constitute "a real data anchor" under Google's current enforcement posture. A "real data anchor" in the post-March-2024 and post-March-2026 environment means operationally-sourced evidence: a job done in that town, a review from that town, or a permit pulled in that town. Statistical data from public APIs is background texture, not an anchor.

Rule 7 (the data pipeline must be a real pipeline, not an LLM prompt) is the most actionable and the one most at risk of being violated at implementation. The recipe correctly prohibits LLM-generated city descriptions. The adversarial risk is that the implementation team treats "auto-generate from Census + NOAA + permit table + OSM" as a proxy for "real data" and publishes indexed pages without any job-history or review data present. The quality gate described in Rule 7 — "if a city row has zero job entries and zero reviews, the page is not published indexed" — must be enforced at the build system level, not as a policy intention.

Rule 10 (incremental rollout, not batch launch) is correct and underemphasized. Launching 30 location pages simultaneously on day one is the pattern most consistent with scaled-content abuse detection by SpamBrain. The recipe buries this in Rule 10 when it should be the first operational instruction.

---

### The Sterling Sky ChatGPT finding — a direct adversarial signal

The search results surfaced a specific finding from Sterling Sky: they tested ChatGPT for hyper-local service area content and "it failed pretty epically." This is not a theoretical concern — the foremost local-SEO research firm tested the exact workflow the recipe proposes (LLM-assisted unique content generation for service area pages) and found it insufficient. This should be prominently noted as a live risk. The recipe's proposed solution to this problem — using real data APIs rather than LLM text generation — is the correct response, but it requires disciplined implementation to avoid LLM-generated prose being used to wrap the real data points.

---

### Summary verdict by component

GENUINELY DEFENSIBLE (passes adversarial test with real data):
- Completed project photos + job description (requires client input, non-negotiable)
- Town-specific reviews mentioning the town (requires client input, non-negotiable)
- Permit jurisdiction identity + link (auto-generatable, valid, requires maintenance)

DEFENSIBLE BUT OVERSTATED (valid texture, not primary differentiators):
- ACS housing-stock data (degrades to county-level for small towns; not a primary differentiator within a metro)
- NOAA climate data (typically identical across a 30-mile metro; supporting texture only)
- Subdivision names (valid when manually verified; OSM auto-population is unreliable)
- Drive time (one-sentence signal; cannot carry a page)

SHOULD BE REMOVED OR DOWNGRADED:
- RSMeans/4BT pricing context (metro-level data, not town-level; reinstates the token-swap problem; remove from "auto-generatable" category)
- LLM-generated city descriptions of any kind (Sterling Sky confirms these fail; the recipe correctly prohibits them but the prohibition must be enforced at the pipeline level)

CORRECTLY TIERED AS TEXTURE:
- Landmarks, HOA references, population data, crew bios

The King Maker system needs a structured intake form (job city, job type, date, photo upload) that feeds directly into the page data layer, or the Tier 1 slots will be empty at launch for the majority of towns.

An explicit policy on what to do with towns that have zero real data at launch — the recipe says 'hold as draft' or 'noindex,' but does not resolve the business tension: a contractor buying a King Maker site expects location pages for all 30 towns on day one. These are the early-warning signals that SpamBrain has flagged the location-page cluster for review.

The data spine (Census + NOAA + permit link + drive time + subdivision list) is legitimately useful as background texture that makes a page more informative than a blank template. It is not sufficient as a primary uniqueness anchor. The architecture should name these two tiers explicitly: Tier A = real operational data (required for indexing), Tier B = public-data texture (added after Tier A is populated).
verdicts.zero_percent_reality:
A literal 0% doorway-page risk is not achievable for a programmatically generated per-town location page system. This is not a defeatist position — it is a structural fact about how Google's systems work and how the policy is enforced.

The honest framing: Google does not guarantee outcomes. The spam policies describe categories of abuse and Google's intent to target them; they do not define a bright compliance line that, once crossed, produces a legal safe harbor. Two sites can have identical architectures and receive different treatment depending on their overall site quality signals, domain history, crawl budget, and the competitive context of their queries. The March 2026 core update data shows that templated location pages were still being penalized two full years after the March 2024 policy codification — meaning enforcement is ongoing and inconsistent, not a one-time sweep.

The realistic risk framing for King Maker:

LOW risk (achievable): A page that has a real completed project photo from that town, a real review mentioning that town or a local neighborhood, the correct permit jurisdiction link, and a manually verified subdivision list is at low risk under Google's current enforcement posture. This is the target, not zero risk.

MODERATE risk (the likely production state at launch): A page that has the auto-generated data spine (Census, NOAA, permit link, drive time, subdivision list) but no real job photo and no local review is at moderate risk. It is meaningfully better than a pure city-swap template but does not clear the "real operational data" bar that Google's 2024-2026 enforcement signals indicate is the operative threshold.

HIGH risk (the failure mode to avoid): A page where the data spine is populated but all prose is LLM-generated, and there is no job photo or local review. This is functionally identical to the doorway pages that lost 63-80% of rankings in the March 2024 and December 2024 enforcement waves.

The correct way to frame the risk target to the client: "We are building a system where each page carries the lowest achievable doorway risk consistent with programmatic generation. That means: indexed pages only for towns with real job history, a public-data texture layer for all pages, and a clear path to strengthen each page as job history accumulates. We cannot promise Google will never flag a page — no one can. We can promise the architecture gives each page a genuine reason to exist beyond keyword capture."

Trying to engineer to 0% risk is also counterproductive: it produces either (a) a system so conservative it publishes only 5-10 indexed pages for a new contractor with limited job history, undermining the value proposition, or (b) pressure to call auto-generated content 'real data' in order to meet a zero-risk standard, which is dishonest and higher-risk than acknowledging the moderate-risk category honestly. The right target is low risk with a documented and enforced quality gate, not zero risk with an unachievable compliance claim.

verdicts.assessment:
The recipe is the best documented public framework for this problem and contains genuinely correct structural thinking. Several components are defensible. However, four of the twelve components re-create the doorway problem in practice if auto-generated without real per-town data, and the recipe undersells how catastrophic that is under Google's current posture. The honest framing: this is a 60-70% doorway-risk-reduction recipe, not a near-zero one, unless the two client-input slots (project photo + local review) are treated as hard publish gates rather than "nice to haves."

COMPONENT-BY-COMPONENT VERDICT:

1. COMPLETED LOCAL PROJECTS / CASE STUDIES WITH PHOTOS — Verdict: GENUINELY UNIQUE, but only if real. The recipe correctly labels this Tier 1. The adversarial problem: a contractor who is just entering a new town has zero jobs there. The recipe says "at least 1 completed project photo from that town" is required before indexing. That is correct, but it means most small contractors launching 30 town pages can legitimately populate maybe 8-12 of them on day one. The remaining 18-22 pages must not be published indexed. The recipe states this but buries it. It should be the first sentence of the entire document, not a footnote in the summary table.

2. TOWN-SPECIFIC CUSTOMER REVIEWS — Verdict: GENUINELY UNIQUE when real, HIGH RISK when synthesized or approximated. The GBP API provides real review text, but most solo contractors have 15-40 total reviews spread across 30 towns, meaning most town pages will have zero or one review. An LLM summarizing "what customers in Apex tend to say" from adjacent reviews is exactly scaled content abuse. The recipe does not call this out loudly enough. The GBP API filter-by-city logic is also fragile: reviewers rarely state their city, so the "filter by reviewer location mention" approach returns a very thin dataset in practice.

3. HOUSING STOCK DATA (Census ACS) — Verdict: STRUCTURALLY UNIQUE DATA, but the copy template is where it collapses. The data itself — median year built, housing units — is genuinely place-specific. However, the recipe's sample copy ("67% of Apex homes were built before 2000") still passes the swap test in spirit: swap "Apex" for "Cary" and a similar sentence is true about Cary. The sentence format is the template; only the number changes. Google's SpamBrain operates at the pattern level, not just the token level. For this to be defensible, the number must drive a qualitatively different recommendation, not just fill a slot. Example that passes: "Apex's median build year of 1998 means most homes there have original R-19 attic insulation — well below current NC code's R-38 requirement, which is the leading cause of HVAC oversizing callbacks in that market." That sentence cannot be replicated by swapping a city name because the logical chain is specific to that number's meaning. The recipe's sample copy does not reach this bar.

4. PERMIT JURISDICTION + PULL REQUIREMENTS — Verdict: GENUINELY UNIQUE if sourced from real municipal data, HIGH RISK if LLM-inferred. Permit authority varies: in Wake County, the Town of Cary issues its own permits while unincorporated areas go through the county. That one sentence is a factual differentiator a homeowner cannot get from a competitor's page. This component is correctly rated. The adversarial risk: the recipe says "fee schedules require scraping or manual maintenance." In practice, fee schedules change annually and scraping municipal PDFs at scale is brittle. If the fee data goes stale and the page says "Cary's roofing permit fee is $85" when it is now $120, the page damages trust rather than building it. Freshness maintenance cost is not acknowledged.

5. LOCAL CLIMATE DATA (NOAA) — Verdict: DATA IS UNIQUE, COPY IS HIGH RISK. Heating degree days and annual rainfall are numerically distinct per city. But the recipe's sample copy — "Apex averages 3,820 heating degree-days per year — your furnace works harder here than in Charlotte" — is the most dangerous component in the entire recipe. Here is why: Charlotte's HDD figure is roughly 3,200, Raleigh is roughly 3,900, Apex is a suburb of Raleigh so its figure is essentially identical to Raleigh. The comparative claim ("harder than Charlotte") is barely distinguishable from a town-swap. More critically, SpamBrain 2024+ has been documented targeting exactly this pattern: a table of climate figures with one number changed per city and an identical sentence structure around it. The climate data is structurally legitimate; the LLM-composed interpretive copy around it is not. To pass the swap test, the copy must do something with the number that is specific to that town's combination of data points — housing stock age plus HDD plus local utility provider — not just restate the number in sentence form.

6. NEIGHBORHOOD / SUBDIVISION NAMES — Verdict: REAL DIFFERENTIATOR, easily abused. Sterling Sky correctly identifies this as a high-value signal. Named subdivisions (Wakefield, Brier Creek, Lochmere) are inherently local and cannot be reused. The adversarial risk: a list of subdivision names with no associated operational content — "We serve Wakefield, Brier Creek, Preston, and Lochmere in Raleigh" — is just a keyword list. Google's 2024 spam updates specifically address "keyword stuffing in structured lists." For subdivision names to carry weight, they must appear in the context of actual operational content: "Our crew serviced 4 homes in Wakefield last spring after the April hailstorm — here are the photos." Without that anchor, the subdivision list is decoration.

7. DRIVE TIME FROM SHOP — Verdict: LEGITIMATE DIFFERENTIATOR, low informational weight. A factual drive time is unique and verifiable. It is also essentially weightless as a standalone content element — it is a one-sentence data point. The recipe correctly places it in Tier 2, but overstates its uniqueness value. "12 minutes from downtown Apex" is more useful as a LocalBusiness schema signal or a Google Maps embed than as page copy. As a text sentence, it contributes minimally to the swap-test defense.

8. LOCAL PRICING CONTEXT — Verdict: MEDIUM-HIGH RISK as described. "Raleigh-area labor rates run ~8% above the NC state average" is a county- or metro-level generalization, not a town-level fact. Wake Forest and Apex have identical cost structures because they pull from the same labor market. This component does not differentiate at the town-page level and should be omitted from town pages entirely unless the contractor has actual job-cost data per town. RSMeans/4BT location factors are county-at-best granularity. Using them to generate per-town pricing copy is exactly the kind of thin differentiation SpamBrain targets.

9. LOCAL LANDMARKS / GEOGRAPHY REFERENCES — Verdict: LOW VALUE, acknowledged correctly. The recipe's own note says Google discounts this if the rest of the page is templated. Correct. A one-line landmark reference is supporting texture at best and keyword stuffing at worst if overused. The recipe's "1-2 sentences max" limit is the right call.

10. LOCAL HOA RULES — Verdict: HIGH VALUE IF REAL, impossible to auto-generate at scale. No machine-readable HOA database exists. The recipe acknowledges this. The suggestion to "list specific active HOAs (verifiable) rather than specific CC&R details" is reasonable but does not add swap-test differentiation — naming HOAs is just another form of listing local proper nouns without operational content.

11. LOCAL CREW MEMBERS / TEAM BIOS — Verdict: STRONGEST E-E-A-T SIGNAL IN THE ENTIRE RECIPE, almost entirely ignored by the recipe's architecture. A named, photographed local technician who lives in or regularly works in that town is inherently unique, Google-verifiable (LinkedIn, GBP, schema Person markup), and maps directly to E-E-A-T's "Experience" and "Authoritativeness" signals for local service. The recipe buries this in Tier 3 as a "no — requires client input" item. That is technically correct but strategically backwards. If a contractor has 3 technicians covering different parts of the service area, each town-page cluster should be anchored to the tech who serves that zone. This is the highest-leverage component in the recipe and is the least developed.

12. LOCAL DEMOGRAPHICS / POPULATION CONTEXT — Verdict: CORRECTLY RATED LOW. "Apex has 65,000 residents" is filler. Correctly placed as secondary and trade-irrelevant without the housing-stock frame.

THE TWO COMPONENTS THAT RE-CREATE THE DOORWAY PROBLEM:

A. Climate copy (Component 5) when auto-generated as sentence templates around NOAA figures. The data is real; the LLM-composed interpretive wrapper is a pattern that SpamBrain recognizes. The entire value of the NOAA data is destroyed if the output is "City X averages Y degree-days — your [equipment] works harder here than in [comparison city]" because that sentence structure is identical across all 30 town pages.

B. Pricing context (Component 8) when applied at town-page granularity using county-level cost factors. Metro-level pricing data does not differentiate Wake Forest from Apex. Publishing per-town pricing pages with functionally identical numbers (both are "Wake County, ~8% above state average") is a direct recreation of the original doorway problem.

WHAT IS MISSING FROM THE RECIPE:

1. A hard publish gate definition. The recipe's most important rule is Rule 4 (only index pages with at least one real data anchor) but it is written as a guideline, not an enforcement mechanism. The build system needs a literal boolean field per town row: has_indexed_job AND has_local_review. If both are false, the page template renders but sets meta robots noindex and the sitemap excludes it. This is architectural, not editorial.

2. Content freshness and rot definition. Permit fee schedules change. Review counts grow. Job photos accumulate. A page that passes the swap test on launch day can degrade to a doorway page 18 months later if the "real data" fields go stale while competitors' pages grow richer. The recipe has no freshness/rot detection rule.

3. Review velocity signal. A town page with one review from 2019 is not materially different from a page with no reviews. Recency matters for both E-E-A-T and user trust. The recipe should specify a minimum freshness threshold for the review slot (e.g., at least one review within the past 24 months) before a page qualifies for indexing.

4. The crew-anchoring architecture. If the contractor's service area is divided into zones served by specific technicians, that geographic crew assignment is the single most powerful auto-generatable uniqueness signal because it is operational truth: John covers the northwest zone (Wake Forest, Youngsville, Rolesville); Maria covers the southwest zone (Apex, Holly Springs, Fuquay-Varina). Each town page in John's zone carries his photo, bio, and license number. This is genuinely unique, verifiable, and cannot be replicated by a competitor without lying.

5. Explicit handling of the "we have never done a job there" scenario. The recipe mentions this but does not specify what the page looks like in draft/noindex state. A contractor launching a site for the first time may have jobs in 8 towns but wants pages for 30. The other 22 pages should not be skeleton templates sitting in the sitemap waiting for Google to crawl them — they should either not exist in the build output or be gated behind a robots.txt disallow until they have content. The recipe treats this as an indexing decision but it is actually a content-generation decision: do not generate a page for a town with no data.

6. Schema as verification layer, not just markup. The recipe correctly lists LocalBusiness + ServiceArea schema as non-optional. But it does not address the verification implication: Google cross-checks schema areaServed claims against GBP service area settings, citation footprint, and review geography. A contractor claiming to serve 30 towns in schema but with GBP reviews from only 5 of them will see their schema claims discounted. The schema and the operational evidence must grow together.

SpamBrain operates at pattern level, not token level. The data is defensible; the LLM-composed wrapper around it is not unless the copy does qualitatively different things with each town's specific number combination — not just fill a slot.

Schema-operational evidence synchronization — GBP service area settings, schema areaServed claims, and review geography must grow together. A contractor claiming 30 towns in schema with reviews from only 5 will have schema claims discounted. The recipe does not address the dependency between schema expansion and operational evidence accumulation.
verdicts.zero_percent_reality: A literal 0% doorway-page risk is not achievable for auto-generated pages. Google does not publish a binary pass/fail test; its systems operate probabilistically. The correct framing for the client is: this recipe, fully implemented with the hard publish gate enforced, the two failing components removed or replaced with real data, and both client-input slots treated as mandatory pre-conditions for indexing, reduces doorway-page penalty risk to a defensibly low level for the pages that are indexed — meaning pages backed by real job history and real reviews. The risk is not zero; it is asymmetric. Pages with real operational data (completed job, local review, permit jurisdiction fact) have low enforcement risk even under Google's aggressive 2024+ posture, because they contain content a real user cannot get from a competitor's page. Pages generated without those anchors carry high enforcement risk regardless of how many data-injected sentences surround them. The practical target to communicate to the client: index only towns where you can answer 'yes' to both — did we do a job there in the past 24 months, and do we have a review from a customer in that town? The auto-generated data spine (Census, NOAA, permit jurisdiction, drive time, subdivision names) supports and contextualizes those anchors but cannot replace them. A 10-page footprint built on real evidence is lower risk and likely higher ranking performance than a 30-page footprint where 20 pages are data-injected templates with no operational history behind them.

result.synthesis:
# Per-Town Location Pages for King Maker: Definitive Strategy

## 1. Honest Framing: What "0% Risk" Actually Means

Literal zero percent doorway-page penalty risk is not achievable for any programmatically generated per-town location page system. This is not a legal hedge — it is a structural fact about how Google's enforcement works.

Google's SpamBrain operates probabilistically across a site's full page set, not as a binary pass/fail per page. Two sites with architecturally identical location pages can receive different treatment based on domain history, GBP signal alignment, review geography, link profile, and the competitive context of their queries. The [March 2024 spam update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies) and [December 2024 spam update case studies (GSQI)](https://www.gsqi.com/marketing-blog/google-december-2024-spam-update-case-studies/) both show ongoing enforcement, not a one-time sweep. The [August 2025 spam update (Sterling Sky)](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/august-2025-spam-algorithm-update/) hit contractor sites again, specifically compounding losses for sites that had old exact-match backlink anchors pointing at thin city pages.

**The honest risk model has three states:**

| State | Page Characteristics | Enforcement Risk |
|---|---|---|
| LOW | Real completed job photo from that town + real review mentioning that town + permit jurisdiction fact + Census housing data cited numerically | Unlikely to trigger automated enforcement; would survive a manual quality review |
| MODERATE | Auto-generated data spine only (Census + NOAA + permit link + drive time + subdivision list) — no job photo, no local review | Better than city-swap boilerplate, but does not clear the "real operational data" bar that post-2024 enforcement signals indicate is operative |
| HIGH | LLM-generated city descriptions around data tokens, no job photo, no local review, structurally identical sentence patterns across 30 pages | Functionally identical to pages that lost 63-80% rankings in March 2024 and December 2024 enforcement waves |

**The defensible target to communicate to clients:** "Built to survive a manual Google quality review." A quality rater looking at the full page set should not be able to reasonably conclude these pages exist primarily to capture [trade] + [city] queries rather than to serve real visitors in those cities. That standard is achievable. Zero risk is not.

The practical floor: **index only towns where you can answer YES to both — did we complete a job there in the past 24 months, AND do we have at least one review from a customer in that town?** A 10-page footprint built on real evidence ranks better and risks less than a 30-page footprint where 20 pages are data-injected templates with no operational history behind them.

---

## 2. Page Content Architecture: The ~80-90% Uniqueness Breakdown

The architecture has two layers: a **Tier A operational data layer** (required for indexing — this is what actually passes the swap test) and a **Tier B public-data texture layer** (supporting context — real, town-specific, but not sufficient alone). Shared template structure fills the remaining scaffold.

The target ratio is: Tier A + Tier B = 40-60% of page word count that genuinely fails the swap test. Shared template (service descriptions, brand list, FAQ boilerplate, contact CTA, schema) can fill the remaining 40-60%. The claim of "80-90% unique" in the brief is achievable in appearance but misleading if Tier A content is absent — you can hit the word-count percentage with Tier B alone and still have a doorway page at the structural level.

### Block-by-Block Architecture

---

#### BLOCK 1: Local Hero / Opening Statement
**Unique-per-town: YES — TIER A REQUIRED**
**Source: Client-provided**
**Risk level: SAFE when real, RISKY when LLM-generated**

The opening 100-150 words must contain at least one statement that fails the swap test by construction. The correct pattern:

> "We replaced 14 roofs in Cary in 2024 — mostly in Lochmere and Preston Forest, where 1990s architectural shingles are hitting their 30-year failure window. Our crew is based 11 minutes from Cary Town Hall."

Compare to the RISKY pattern:

> "Cary NC homeowners face unique roofing challenges given the area's climate and aging housing stock." [RISKY — LLM boilerplate, passes swap test, flagged by SpamBrain]

**Implementation:** `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].intro` must require a job-count field (`jobCount`) and a primary subdivision reference (`primarySubdivision`). The template renders these as inline facts, not as LLM-written prose. If `jobCount` is null and `primarySubdivision` is null, the page does not publish indexed.

---

#### BLOCK 2: Completed Project Evidence
**Unique-per-town: YES — TIER A REQUIRED**
**Source: Client-provided (non-negotiable)**
**Risk level: SAFE (irreproducible by construction)**

One or more completed job entries from that specific town: real photo (geo-tagged EXIF preferred), job type, approximate neighborhood or street descriptor (no full street address required), approximate date, scope of work.

> "April 2024 — Complete shingle replacement, Haddon Hall subdivision, Apex. 2,400 sq ft, GAF Timberline HDZ in Charcoal, pulled Wake County permit #2024-04-8817."

This is structurally undefeatable. A job photo on Creekwood Drive in Apex cannot be reused in Holly Springs. Permit numbers are verifiable. This is the single component that most clearly satisfies Google's [E-E-A-T "Experience" signal](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/12/google-raters-guidelines-e-e-a-t) for local service pages.

**DataPins pattern reference:** [DataPins documents](https://www.datapins.com/seo-for-multiple-cities/) that contractor technician check-ins at each jobsite — generating a geo-tagged pin with real photo + job description + schema markup that auto-publishes to the city page — produce content that is literally unreplicable by competitors. This is the model to implement or approximate.

**Minimum for indexing:** 1 job entry, completed within the past 24 months.

---

#### BLOCK 3: Local Customer Reviews
**Unique-per-town: YES — TIER A REQUIRED**
**Source: GBP API extraction (partial auto) + client tagging**
**Risk level: SAFE when real; RISKY when synthesized or approximated**

Pull from Google Business Profile API filtering for reviews that mention the town name, a local neighborhood, or a street. Display 1-3 reviews. Schema `Review` markup on each.

The adversarial reality: most solo contractors have 15-40 total reviews spread across 30 towns. Many reviews say "great job" with no location detail. The usable subset per town is often zero at launch.

**Correct implementation:**
- `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].reviews` — array populated from GBP API pull filtered by reviewer city OR keyword match (town name, subdivision name, cross-reference with job addresses)
- If array is empty AND no job photo exists → page does not publish indexed. Full stop.
- If array has a review but it does not mention the town → include it but do not treat it as a primary swap-test differentiator; it is supporting trust signal only

**What is explicitly RISKY and must never happen:** An LLM summarizing "what customers in Apex tend to say" from adjacent town reviews. This is scaled content abuse by definition.

---

#### BLOCK 4: Local Housing Stock Context
**Unique-per-town: YES (for non-metro towns) / DEGRADED (for towns sharing a Census grain)**
**Source: Auto-generated — [Census ACS 5-Year API](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/acs-5year.html), variables B25035_001E (median year built) and B25001_001E (housing units)**
**Risk level: SAFE when the number drives qualitatively different copy; RISKY when used as a sentence template**

The data is genuinely place-specific at the Census "place" geography level. The risk is how it is rendered.

**RISKY pattern (template sentence, SpamBrain detects):**
> "67% of Apex homes were built before 2000 — aging HVAC systems are the #1 service call here."

**SAFE pattern (the number drives a qualitatively different recommendation):**
> "Apex's median home build year is 1998 (Census ACS 2022). That means most homes are running original R-19 attic insulation — well below NC's current R-38 code requirement — which is the leading cause of HVAC oversizing callbacks we see in that market."

The difference: the SAFE pattern uses the specific number to produce a town-specific recommendation. Swap Apex for Cary (median build 2003) and the recommendation changes — R-22 original insulation, a different failure pattern. The RISKY pattern produces the same sentence regardless of the number.

**Degradation rule:** For small NC municipalities where Census does not publish at the place level (population under ~20,000), the ACS data resolves to the county level. If Apex and Holly Springs return the same county-level median year built, this block is suppressed or merged on the hub page — it does not differentiate two town pages sharing the same grain. Build a data-grain checker into the pipeline: `if town_ACS_value == adjacent_town_ACS_value → suppress_block`.

---

#### BLOCK 5: Permit Jurisdiction + Pull Requirements
**Unique-per-town: YES — TIER B (auto-generatable, requires maintenance)**
**Source: Static lookup table, manually built and annually verified**
**Risk level: SAFE when accurate; trust-negative when stale**

This is the strongest auto-generatable differentiator in the entire architecture. The permit authority for Cary is the Town of Cary (not Wake County). That sentence is factually wrong if you substitute Holly Springs (which uses the county), and a homeowner can verify it at [Wake County Permits](https://www.wake.gov/departments-government/permits-and-inspections) or the [Town of Cary permit portal](https://data.townofcary.org/explore/dataset/permit-applications/).

Build a 30-row lookup table: `town → permit_authority, permit_office_url, typical_inspection_timeline, contractor_license_threshold`. This is a one-time manual build that degrades without annual review.

**Maintenance requirement:** The King Maker system must include an annual permit-table verification step. A page that claims "Cary permits are inspected within 3 business days" when the current timeline is 5 days is worse than no claim — it is factually incorrect and discoverable by any homeowner.

---

#### BLOCK 6: Local Climate Context
**Unique-per-town: DEGRADED WITHIN METRO — treat as Tier B supporting texture, not primary differentiator**
**Source: Auto-generated — [NOAA NCEI Climate Normals API](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/api/v2)**
**Risk level: RISKY if used as primary differentiator within the Raleigh metro**

The adversarial finding here is severe and underweighted in the source research: NOAA degree-day data for Apex, Cary, Holly Springs, Fuquay-Varina, and Morrisville all resolve to the same RDU airport weather station. HDD and CDD figures across these five pages would be numerically identical. Google's crawl-time page comparison across a domain will detect this. "Apex averages 3,820 heating degree-days" and "Cary averages 3,820 heating degree-days" — same sentence with a different city token — is definitionally a doorway pattern.

**Correct use:** Use NOAA data only where towns are in genuinely different climate zones (Raleigh metro vs. coastal NC vs. mountain NC). Within a 30-mile suburban service radius, suppress this block or use it only to make a cross-regional comparison that is actually meaningful (e.g., comparing to Charlotte or Asheville, where the numbers are meaningfully different). Do not repeat nearly identical HDD/CDD sentences across 15 suburban town pages.

---

#### BLOCK 7: Subdivision / Neighborhood Names
**Unique-per-town: YES when operationally anchored; RISKY as a standalone keyword list**
**Source: Manually verified seed list per town + cross-reference with job history**
**Risk level: SAFE when names appear in operational context; RISKY as an OSM-generated keyword list**

[Sterling Sky's research](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/how-to-create-unique-and-helpful-service-area-pages-for-local-businesses/) identifies subdivision names as a high-performing uniqueness signal specifically because they are locally resonant and pass the swap test. "Wakefield Plantation" cannot appear on the Holly Springs page.

The adversarial risk: a list generated from OpenStreetMap Overpass without manual verification will produce errors. OSM neighborhood tags in NC suburbs are inconsistently populated. A page that names a subdivision that does not exist, or misspells an HOA name, is an E-E-A-T liability.

**Correct implementation:**
- Seed list: manually build a 4-6 subdivision list per town, verified against county GIS parcel data or the municipality's own maps
- Operational anchor requirement: each named subdivision should appear in the context of a job reference or service mention, not just as a standalone list. "We've worked in Wakefield, Brier Creek, and Carpenter Village — neighborhoods where 2000s vinyl siding is starting to show UV fading and impact damage" passes the swap test. A bullet list "Serving: Wakefield, Brier Creek, Carpenter Village, North Ridge" is keyword stuffing

---

#### BLOCK 8: Drive Time from Nearest Crew Base
**Unique-per-town: YES — but low informational weight**
**Source: Auto-generated — Google Maps Distance Matrix API or [OSRM](http://project-osrm.org/)**
**Risk level: SAFE as supporting texture; insufficient as primary differentiator**

"We're 11 minutes from Cary Town Hall" is a factual, verifiable, town-specific sentence. It also contributes minimally to a swap-test defense when it is one of only a few differentiating elements. Eleven pages each with a single drive-time sentence that differs only in a number and a city name is structurally token-swap content.

Use it as supporting texture in the opening block or in a "Why choose us in [Town]" section, embedded within broader operational content — never as a standalone uniqueness carrier.

---

#### BLOCK 9: Local Pricing Context [REMOVE FROM AUTO-GENERATED LAYER]
**DO NOT USE as a town-level auto-generated component**

RSMeans and [4BT location cost factors](https://4bt.us/national-average-cost-data-and-locatio-factoring/) operate at metro or county granularity. "Raleigh-area labor rates run ~8% above the NC state average" applies identically to Apex, Cary, Holly Springs, Morrisville, and Wake Forest. Every page in a 30-mile radius carries the same sentence with only the city token changed. This is the canonical doorway pattern.

Replace with: actual per-job cost ranges from the contractor's own CRM data (`LOCATION_CONTENT[town].typicalJobRange`), or omit pricing entirely from town pages and handle it on service pages where it is contextually appropriate.

---

#### BLOCK 10: Local Crew Assignment (UNDERUTILIZED — promote to Tier A)
**Unique-per-town: YES — strongest E-E-A-T signal in the entire architecture**
**Source: Client-provided (contractor CRM zone assignments)**
**Risk level: SAFE — verifiable, operational, irreproducible**

If the contractor's service area is divided into zones served by specific technicians, each town-page cluster anchored to the technician who primarily serves that zone is the highest-leverage uniqueness signal available. A named, photographed technician with a license number who lives in or regularly works in that town satisfies Google's [E-E-A-T "Experience" and "Authoritativeness" signals](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/12/google-raters-guidelines-e-e-a-t) directly.

"John Martinez (NC Roofing License #51432) covers our Wake Forest, Youngsville, and Rolesville routes. He's been doing roofs in North Wake County for 11 years." That sentence cannot be replicated for another town without being false.

**Implementation:** `LOCATION_CONTENT[zone].primaryTech` object with name, photo, license number, years in area, zone towns. One tech can cover 4-6 towns. This is generatable from a single client-provided input that amortizes across the entire zone cluster.

---

#### BLOCK 11: Trade-Specific FAQ (Town-Specific Entry Required)
**Unique-per-town: PARTIAL — at least 1 of 4-5 FAQ entries must be town-specific**
**Source: Mix of static template (shared FAQs) + `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].faq` (town-specific entry)**
**Risk level: SAFE when answers reference real local variables; RISKY when LLM-generated without local data**

Shared FAQ entries (what does a roof replacement cost, how long does it take, what brands do you use) can appear on every page without penalty — they are the 40-60% shared scaffold.

The town-specific FAQ entry must reference a real local variable. Examples that pass the swap test:

- "Do you pull Wake County permits for Apex jobs, or does the Town of Apex issue them?" → Answer references the actual permit authority lookup
- "Our HOA in Regency Park requires specific shingle colors — can you work within those restrictions?" → Answer names the specific HOA and addresses it
- "We had hail damage in the April 2024 storm — do you work with State Farm adjusters in Wake County?" → References a real storm event and county

**RISKY pattern:** "How much does HVAC replacement cost in Cary NC?" answered with "HVAC replacement in Cary NC typically costs $X,XXX-$Y,YYY depending on unit size and complexity." This is the same answer for every city, and LLM-generated FAQ responses that merely insert a city name are [explicitly flagged in Glenn Gabe's December 2024 case studies](https://www.gsqi.com/marketing-blog/google-december-2024-spam-update-case-studies/) as a primary scaled-content-abuse signal ("every PAA turned into a heading").

---

#### BLOCK 12: Shared Scaffold (40-60% of page — NOT doorway material)
**Shared across all town pages — explicitly acceptable**

These blocks are the same on every town page. Google's doorway policy does not penalize shared structural content — it penalizes pages where the shared content is ALL the content.

- Service descriptions (what the trade service covers, process steps)
- Brand/material lists (GAF, Owens Corning, Carrier, Trane, etc.)
- Licensing and insurance credentials (contractor's NC license number)
- Contact CTA and click-to-call (town-specific phone number routing is a plus but not required)
- Generic trust signals (BBB accreditation, years in business)
- Navigation and footer

**Rule:** The shared scaffold is safe precisely because the Tier A and Tier B blocks above it provide the swap-test defense. Remove the Tier A content and the shared scaffold becomes a doorway page by itself.

---

### Summary Table

| Block | Unique-per-Town | Source | Risk if Auto-LLM | Min for Index |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opening statement (job count, subdivision) | YES — Tier A | Client CRM | HIGH — boilerplate | Required |
| Completed project evidence | YES — Tier A | Client photos + permit records | Cannot fake | Required (1 job, 24 mo) |
| Local customer reviews | YES — Tier A | GBP API + client tagging | HIGH if synthesized | Required (1 review, 18 mo) |
| Housing stock data (Census ACS) | YES (with caveats) | Census API — cited figure | MED — template sentence | Recommended |
| Permit jurisdiction | YES | Static lookup table | SAFE if from table, RISKY if inferred | Recommended |
| Climate data (NOAA) | NO within metro — suppress | NOAA API | HIGH within metro | Do not use for same-MSA pages |
| Subdivision names | YES when anchored | Manual seed list | MED — keyword list if not anchored | Recommended (anchored) |
| Drive time | YES — low weight | OSRM / Maps API | SAFE — one sentence | Supporting texture only |
| Pricing context (metro-level) | NO — remove | RSMeans / 4BT | HIGH — metro-wide identical | Do not use at town level |
| Crew zone assignment | YES — Tier A if available | Client CRM | Cannot fake | Promote to required |
| Town-specific FAQ entry | YES — 1 required | `LOCATION_CONTENT[town].faq` | HIGH if LLM-generated | Required (1 entry) |
| Shared scaffold | NO — shared | Template | Acceptable | Structural requirement |

---

## 3. Rules for Safe Auto-Generation

### Rule 1 — The Swap Test is the Go/No-Go Gate
Before any spoke page goes live indexed, apply the swap test: replace the town name with a different town. If the page still reads as useful and accurate, it is a doorway page. Every indexed page must contain at least one block of content that fails the swap test — content that is factually specific to that town and cannot be reused elsewhere without being wrong or meaningless.

### Rule 2 — Tier A Operational Data is the Only Durable Index Gate
The auto-generated public-data spine (Census, NOAA, drive time, permit jurisdiction, subdivision list) is Tier B supporting texture. It is NOT sufficient as a standalone indexing gate. The Tier A gate is binary:

```
has_indexed_job: bool  // 1+ completed job in this town, within 24 months
has_local_review: bool // 1+ review mentioning this town or local neighborhood, within 18 months
```

If either field is false → page builds with `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">` and is excluded from `sitemap-locations.xml`. This is a build-system enforcement rule, not an editorial guideline.

### Rule 3 — Template Ratio and Absolute Word Floor
The shared scaffold can fill up to 60% of the page. The unique Tier A + Tier B content must constitute at least 40%. More importantly, the absolute unique-content word count must be at minimum 300 words — because a 400-word page that is 40% unique contains only 160 words of unique content, which is not sufficient informational depth. [BrightLocal's guidance](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/location-pages/) targets 800-1,500+ words of substantive content per indexed location page.

### Rule 4 — Page Count is Constrained by Job History, Not Keyword Opportunity
| Indexed page tier | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Tier 1 (index immediately) | 3+ completed jobs in 24 months AND 2+ local reviews |
| Tier 2 (index after content is staged) | 1-2 jobs in 24 months OR 1 local review (not both missing) |
| Do not index | Zero jobs in 24 months AND zero local reviews |

For a solo contractor launching a new King Maker site, this typically produces 8-15 immediately indexable pages and 10-20 pages in noindex staging. That is the correct production state on day one.

Maximum indexed page count for a small contractor (one physical location, 30-mile radius): 15-25 high-quality pages outperform 40+ thin pages in every documented case. [Plumbing Webmasters (1,000+ contractor campaigns)](https://www.plumbingwebmasters.com/plumber-city-page-seo/) recommends a strict 15-city maximum with real job documentation.

### Rule 5 — Only Index Towns Where You Have Real Service History
Do not generate indexed pages for towns the contractor has never served. Towns outside active job history get:
- An `areaServed` entry in root schema
- An anchor link on the `/service-area` hub
- A draft/noindex page in the build output (to be promoted when jobs accumulate)

This is not conservatism — it is the architecture that makes the whole system honest. Without this rule, the data-spine approach is a sophisticated-looking doorway campaign.

### Rule 6 — LLM Prose Must Never Wrap Data Without a Human Review Step
The pipeline may use LLM assistance to draft prose around real data points. But the prose must then be reviewed and edited by a human (or the contractor) before publishing. The distinguishing signal between operational content and scaled-content abuse is whether the prose reflects genuine knowledge of that specific market. [Sterling Sky tested ChatGPT for hyper-local service area content and it "failed pretty epically"](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/how-to-create-unique-and-helpful-service-area-pages-for-local-businesses/) — the output was fluent but indistinguishable from the city-swap boilerplate the March 2024 update targeted.

The correct prose pattern: "We replaced 34 roofs in Apex in 2024, mostly in Haddon Hall and Regency Park subdivisions, where 1990s architectural shingles are failing at the 30-year mark." This is operator-authored experience. It cannot come from an LLM that has never been to Apex.

### Rule 7 — Incremental Launch, Not Batch
Never launch all location pages simultaneously. The correct sequence:

1. Identify the 6-12 towns with highest job density and strongest review concentration
2. Launch those pages first, fully staged with all Tier A content
3. Submit to Search Console via URL Inspection; monitor Coverage and Performance for 3-4 weeks
4. Add remaining towns in batches of 5-8 as job and review data accumulates
5. Never launch a new town page until its Tier A gate is satisfied

Launching 30 near-identical pages in one sitemap submission is a pattern consistent with [SpamBrain's scaled-content-abuse detection](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies).

### Rule 8 — Data Freshness Policy
- Census ACS data: cite the vintage year inline ("Census ACS 2022 5-Year Estimates"). Refresh annually when new ACS data publishes.
- NOAA climate normals: cite the 1991-2020 normals period. These update on a 10-year cycle.
- Permit jurisdiction data: annual verification required. Flag unverified entries with a stale date so they are suppressed from rendering until re-verified.
- Job data: only jobs within the past 24 months count toward the indexing gate. Older jobs may appear in a "project history" section but cannot substitute for recent evidence.

### Rule 9 — Metro-Radius Deduplication Check
Before treating any auto-generated data block as a uniqueness signal, run a deduplication check: if the value for Town A equals the value for Town B (same Census grain, same NOAA station, same permit authority), suppress the block from both pages or render it only on the hub page. This is especially critical for the Raleigh metro cluster where 8-10 suburbs share the same MSA data sources.

### Rule 10 — Quarterly Swap-Test Audit
Run a structural similarity check across all live spoke pages quarterly. If any two pages score above 70% similarity (excluding shared scaffold), merge them into one richer page or differentiate the thinner one. This is the ongoing quality-maintenance mechanism that prevents content rot.

---

## 4. Technical Architecture

### URL Structure: Hub-and-Spoke

```
/service-area                          ← hub (keep — retains all existing equity)
/locations/raleigh                     ← spoke
/locations/cary
/locations/apex
/locations/wake-forest
/locations/holly-springs
```

**Rationale for `/locations/{town-slug}` over flat `/raleigh-hvac`:**
- The nested path signals geographic sub-taxonomy explicitly to crawlers
- Avoids slug collisions across multi-trade clients in the same King Maker system
- The hub page at `/service-area` retains all equity accumulated during the consolidation period — do not delete it or redirect it away

**Slug rules:**
- Lowercase, hyphenated, NC town name only: `/locations/wake-forest`
- No trade name in the slug: `/locations/apex` not `/locations/apex-roofing-nc`
- Canonical on each spoke: `<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/locations/apex" />`
- Consistent trailing slash policy — pick one and enforce sitewide

### Schema: LocalBusiness + Service + areaServed

**Root node (homepage only — do not duplicate on spoke pages):**

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "RoofingContractor",
  "name": "Acme Roofing",
  "url": "https://example.com",
  "telephone": "+1-919-555-0100",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "123 Main St",
    "addressLocality": "Raleigh",
    "addressRegion": "NC",
    "postalCode": "27601",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "areaServed": [
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Raleigh"},
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Cary"},
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Apex"},
    {"@type": "City", "name": "Wake Forest"}
  ]
}
```

**Per-spoke node (each `/locations/{town}` page):**

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Service",
  "name": "Roof Replacement in Apex NC",
  "serviceType": "Roof Replacement",
  "provider": {
    "@type": "RoofingContractor",
    "name": "Acme Roofing",
    "url": "https://example.com"
  },
  "areaServed": {
    "@type": "City",
    "name": "Apex",
    "containedInPlace": {
      "@type": "State",
      "name": "North Carolina"
    }
  }
}
```

**Critical schema rules:**
- Use `areaServed` (current Schema.org). The `serviceArea` property is deprecated as of Schema.org v7+ — do not use it
- Do NOT add a second full `LocalBusiness` node on spoke pages — phantom multi-location signals confuse GBP alignment
- Do NOT embed a `PostalAddress` for towns where the contractor has no physical office
- Use the most specific `@type` available: `RoofingContractor`, `HVACBusiness`, `Plumber`, `Electrician`
- Schema claims and GBP service area settings must grow together: do not claim 30 towns in schema when GBP reviews exist for only 5

### Internal Linking

**Hub → Spokes:** `/service-area` links to every active (indexed) spoke via a service-area grid. Anchor text: "Roofing in {Town}" — keyword + city, not bare city name.

**Spoke → Hub:** Every spoke links back to the hub: "See our full roofing service area →". This reciprocal link prevents spoke pages from becoming isolated doorway-style dead ends — the direct pattern Google's [2015 doorway policy](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2015/03/an-update-on-doorway-pages) identifies as a flag.

**Spoke → Adjacent Spokes:** Link to 2-3 geographically adjacent towns only (within 10 miles or same county). Do not build a full cross-link matrix — that dilutes equity and looks manipulative.

**Service pages → Spokes:** `/services/roof-replacement` includes a "Towns We Serve" section linking to 4-6 highest-volume spoke pages. Creates cross-dimensional links (service → location) that strengthen topical authority.

### Reversing the 308 Redirects

The existing 308 redirects (`/locations/{town}` → `/service-area#{town}`) were treated by Google as permanent canonical signals. Equity was consolidated to `/service-area`. Reversal requires:

1. Google to re-crawl the restored URL
2. Google to re-evaluate canonical (page now exists, no redirect)
3. Google to re-associate any inbound links from the old spoke URLs
4. A 4-8 week equity reconsolidation period during which spoke pages may rank weakly

**Batched reversal protocol:**

| Week | Action |
|---|---|
| 0 | Verify Tier A content for top 5 revenue towns satisfies the index gate |
| 1 | Remove 308 for those 5 towns, restore `/locations/{town}`, add to `sitemap-locations.xml`, submit via Search Console URL Inspection |
| 2-3 | Monitor Search Console Coverage + Performance for those 5 URLs |
| 4 | If indexing confirmed, proceed with next batch of 5-8 towns |
| Ongoing | Never restore a 308 until that town's Tier A gate is satisfied |

Towns not yet ready: leave 308 in place. Do not return 200 with thin content — that is worse than a redirect, because a thin 200 is actively crawled and indexed as low-quality content.

### Sitemap Governance

Separate the locations sitemap for independent management:

```xml
<!-- sitemap-index.xml -->
<sitemapindex>
  <sitemap><loc>/sitemap-core.xml</loc></sitemap>
  <sitemap><loc>/sitemap-locations.xml</loc></sitemap>
</sitemapindex>
```

`sitemap-locations.xml` includes a spoke URL only after it passes the Tier A gate. Including thin pages in the sitemap signals to Google that you consider them canonical and indexable — it does not protect you, it flags you.

**Staging protocol:**
1. Page built but below Tier A gate → serve 200 + `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">` + exclude from sitemap
2. Tier A gate passes → remove noindex tag + add to `sitemap-locations.xml` + submit in Search Console
3. Never block via `robots.txt` — that prevents Google from reading the noindex directive
